chapter.chapter:
Alice came up to the mouth of it and stopped short, one foot among the loose earth at the brink. It was all very well for a rabbit to pop down—a rabbit is made for holes, and no doubt knows all the turnings—but below Alice there was nothing to be seen except blackness. It suddenly occurred to her that going down would be by far the easiest part of the adventure: there were no stairs that she could discover, and no convenient roots for coming up again, and it would be a very ridiculous thing to be obliged to remain at the bottom, calling to her sister to fetch a ladder.

So, though she was still burning with curiosity, she dropped upon her knees in the grass, put her hands round her mouth, and called as politely as she could into the darkness, “Oh, if you please, Mr. Rabbit, will you wait a minute?”

The words went down in a very curious manner, growing smaller and smaller, as if they were hurrying after him themselves—“wait a minute—wait a minute—wait—”—and then there was a scrabbling, and a great deal of indistinct grumbling, as when somebody is interrupted in the middle of being in a hurry.

Presently the earth at the mouth stirred. First came a white scut and two hind feet, then a waistcoat drawn very tight with the effort, and last of all two long ears laid flat back; for the Rabbit was obliged to come out backwards, there being, as it afterwards explained, no proper room for turning in a professional hurry. It got upon its feet, shook the mould from its waistcoat before her, and looked as much offended as if Alice had personally invented lateness.

“Now,” said the Rabbit, “you have made me later than I was, which is a thing nobody ought to do without an introduction.”

“I beg your pardon,” said Alice. “I didn’t mean to stop you altogether. I only wanted to ask—”

“People in a hurry are always being asked questions,” said the Rabbit. “If questions were left till people had arrived, answers would be much more punctual. As it is, I shall be late.”

“But what are you late for?” Alice asked.

“For four o’clock, to be sure.”

“And what is to happen at four o’clock?”

“The garden on the other side of this hedge is to be opened. I have to go down, and along, and up the passage, and unlock the door from its own side. A door cannot be opened respectably unless somebody is where the door expects him.”

It took the watch out as it spoke, and turned it over, as if the figures might have improved while it was not looking. As it jerked at the chain in great vexation, something bright slipped from a link, made a little glittering arc in the sunlight, and landed among the daisies almost at Alice’s knees; but the Rabbit was too much engaged with its watch to notice it, and Alice only thought a gnat had flashed past.

“Three minutes to four,” said the Rabbit. Then it felt the chain suddenly light, patted its waistcoat-pocket twice, and gave a small squeak of horror. “My key! It’s gone!”

“I don’t see how it can be my fault,” said Alice.

“Your calling made me turn round in a place meant only for going straight on, and the key was knocked off against a root.”

“If it was knocked off down there,” said Alice, “it cannot very well be looking for itself up here.”

“Everything that is lost is somewhere,” said the Rabbit severely. “It is much more convenient when somewhere happens to be here. Come—we must find it. You have hands, which are useful for parting grass, though not, apparently, for letting well alone.”

So they went down on their knees and searched. The Rabbit kept consulting its watch, and saying “Later and later!” in a tone that made the daisies seem partly to blame. Alice, as she parted the stems, fell almost without thinking of it into threading the daisies together, partly because her fingers were accustomed to the work, and partly because she thought that, if she made a chain as she went, she should know which grass had been looked under and which had not. “That,” said the Rabbit, watching her, “is a slow way of being quick.”

“It’s quicker than looking in the same place three times,” said Alice; and at that moment her hand closed upon something small and warm from the sun under a leaf. “Here it is!”

The Rabbit snatched at it, but Alice held it a moment at arm’s length, for a new idea had come to her. All along the foot of the hedge the roots went in and out like the ribs of a boat, and among them, half smothered in creepers, was a door—not much more than fifteen inches high—with a brass keyhole that seemed remarkably wide awake. “Why do you go down the hole,” she said, “when there is a door on this side?”

“Because this is the outside,” said the Rabbit. “One doesn’t begin a door at the wrong end.”

“Keyholes can’t tell which end they are looked at from,” said Alice, and she put the key in and turned it before the Rabbit could get its paws free from its watch. To her great delight it fitted. The little door swung inward.

A breath of cooler air came out, smelling of leaves after rain and of flowers in the sun. Alice knelt and looked through. Beyond were trim paths, beds of bright blossoms nodding gravely in the heat, and fountains throwing up clear water that fell back with a pleasant splash. It was exactly the sort of garden one longs to walk in after sitting a long while doing nothing; only the doorway was so low that, though she could get her head through easily enough, her shoulders declined to follow. “It would be no use,” she said mournfully, “to send my head into a garden without me.”

“There is a provision,” said the Rabbit, “for visitors of an inconvenient size.” It flattened its ears, squeezed through the opening with a great air of importance, and presently reappeared pushing before it, by the neck, a little bottle. There was a paper label round it, with the words “DRINK ME” beautifully printed in large letters. Set into the thickness of the hedge, just inside, Alice could see a narrow niche where the bottle belonged.

“It isn’t marked *poison*,” she said, turning it round.

“Labels,” said the Rabbit, “are not meant as invitations to everybody.”

Still, Alice was not going to taste it in a hurry; she had read too many histories of children who came to harm by not remembering simple rules. So she only put out the tip of her tongue at first. It tasted of cherries and custard, and then, very oddly, of pine-apple, and then of something unmistakably like hot buttered toast. “It can’t be poison with toast in it,” she said to herself; and, the Rabbit tapping its foot beside the open door, she raised the bottle and drank.

What happened next was so quick that the hedge seemed to be growing faster than any hedge had a right to do. The roots rose up like arches, the grass-blades stood round her tall and green, and the bottle, which she had set down carefully for fear of spilling it, towered beside her like a milk-jug at a giant’s breakfast. In a moment or two Alice found she had stopped shrinking; she was no taller now than the daisies she had been threading. The Rabbit’s watch hung above her nearly as large as a cart-wheel, and went tick, tick, tick, in a solemn, enormous manner.

“Now, now!” cried the Rabbit. “Mind you come while it’s open!” It shoved the bottle back into its niche, whisked through with the key, to put everything, as it said, upon the proper side; and the little door, which was hung upon a spring of twisted creeper, clicked to behind it.

Alice was beginning to say “But—” when the ground gave a soft thud under her, and then another. A voice, so large and distant that it seemed to come down the sky, called, “Alice! Alice!” Her sister had shut the book and come across the field to look for her. In another second she was close to the hedge, standing with the book under her arm and shading her eyes as she searched the grass, entirely unaware that Alice, crouching beneath a broad daisy leaf beside her shoe, was calling up “Here I am! Here I am!” as loudly as ever she could. To her sister it evidently sounded no more than a grasshopper stirring in the warm grass.

“She cannot be hiding,” her sister said, half to herself, glancing doubtfully at the dark mouth of the hole. “And she has too much sense to go down there.” Then she moved on a few paces along the hedge, with her back turned, to look round the other side.

Behind Alice there was a faint click among the roots. A leaf that was not only a leaf moved outward, an eye and a long ear appeared, and the door stood open again from within, the Rabbit holding it with one paw. “Now, if you please,” it whispered, “or not till next four o’clock. Doors dislike being kept waiting at their own opening.”

Alice looked up at her sister’s retreating back, and down at the strip of sunlight lying across the threshold. Then she ran as fast as her small legs could carry her between the grass-stems, climbed over a root as rough as a stile, and stepped over the sill. The bright flower-beds were nodding above her, the cool sound of the fountain was close at hand; and as the Rabbit let the door swing to behind them, the field, the hedge, and her sister’s shoe were shut out all at once.

chapter.chapter:
Scrooge did not answer at once. He looked at his nephew, as if Christmas dinner and all its train of expenses were already entered, duly cast up, and found wanting, in some invisible ledger. He looked at the clerk's miserable attempt at a fire, now quite extinguished by that unfortunate burst of applause. He looked at the frost upon the window, and at the brown fog pressing against it from without.

“A dinner,” said Scrooge at last, “will cost me nothing at your house.”

His nephew, who had prepared himself for half-an-hour's more argument, was struck so dumb by this unexpected beginning that he could only repeat, “Uncle!”

“You are always asking,” said Scrooge. “You are always telling me what good Christmas has done you. Much good it has done you, with your rent to pay, and a wife to keep, and not a scrap of gold or silver the more in your pocket for it. I will come and see. I will come, if it is only to know what such wisdom feeds upon. There! That is an end of the invitation for this year, and all years to come, I hope.”

He rose slowly, put out his own lean hand, and took the nephew's warm one in it, as if the thing had been a bond to be duly witnessed and registered.

“I will dine with you to-morrow,” said Scrooge.

“Uncle! My dear uncle!” cried his nephew, holding the cold fingers fast, in the mere excess of his delight. “You will make us happy indeed. My wife will be--”

“There! There!” said Scrooge, drawing his hand away, as though it smarted. “No compliments. I make a bargain when I choose, but I don't stand to have it talked into a favour. What time?”

“Four, uncle. Any time. Come when you will.”

“Four then. I am not a man to be kept waiting for my dinner by fiddling and fine speeches. And mind! I stay for none of your games afterwards. No blindman's-buff, no forfeits, no music after meat. I have seen enough of that folly in my time without paying for a fresh exhibition.”

“You shall do precisely as you like,” returned his nephew. “You shall sit by the fire, and scowl at the pudding if it pleases you, and we shall be glad to have you.”

The clerk in the Tank, forgetting himself a second time, emitted an approving sound, something between a cough and a small cheer. Scrooge turned upon him with such promptitude, that he subsided into his white comforter, and appeared to become all at once deeply interested in the letter before him.

“Let me hear another sound from you,” said Scrooge, “whether of Christmas or anything else, and you will no doubt have leisure enough to make it in the street. You're quite a powerful speaker yourself, sir,” he added, addressing his nephew again, “the moment anything can be got for nothing by talking. I wonder you don't go into Parliament, where there's more pay for it.”

His nephew laughed a good-humoured laugh, and, putting on his hat, declared that he would carry the tidings home before Scrooge had time to change his mind. “I wouldn't change your mind for the Bank of England,” said he, “but mine is made up, and I dare say you know it. To-morrow at four, uncle. A merry Christmas to you, in earnest this time, whether you will or no.”

He stopped at the outer door to wish the clerk the compliments of the season, and received them cordially, poor shivering fellow; though he was colder than Scrooge, and had a great deal less to make him warm. The clerk opened the door to let him out, and, in the act of doing so, very nearly let his heart out too; for two other persons, who were waiting in the passage, passed briskly in. They were portly gentlemen, pleasant to behold, though somewhat blown by the fog and earnest in their looks, and they now stood, with their hats off, in Scrooge's office, having books and papers in their hands.

They had met the nephew on the threshold, and, having recognised him (for there are few people who could meet that face at Christmas-time and not know its errand), had received from him, before the door closed, a contribution so cheerful, and, considering the narrowness of his means, so liberal, that Scrooge, who overheard the chink and the gentlemen's thanks, soured visibly at the sound.

“Scrooge and Marley's, I believe,” said one of the gentlemen, referring to his list. “Have I the pleasure of addressing Mr. Scrooge, or Mr. Marley?”

“Mr. Marley has been dead these seven years,” Scrooge replied. “He died seven years ago this very night.”

“We have no doubt his liberality is well represented by his surviving partner,” said the gentleman, presenting his credentials.

Scrooge frowned, shook his head, and handed them back again, as if they burnt him.

“At this festive season of the year, Mr. Scrooge,” said the gentleman, taking up a pen, “it is more than usually desirable that we should make some slight provision for the Poor and destitute, who suffer greatly at the present time. Many thousands are in want of common necessaries; hundreds of thousands are in want of common comforts, sir.”

“Are there no prisons?” asked Scrooge.

“Plenty of prisons,” said the gentleman, laying down the pen again.

“And the Union workhouses? Are they still in operation?”

“They are. Still,” returned the gentleman, “I wish I could say they were not.”

“The Treadmill and the Poor Law are in full vigour, then?” said Scrooge.

“Both very busy, sir.”

“Oh! I was afraid, from what you said at first, that something had occurred to stop them in their useful course,” said Scrooge. “I'm very glad to hear it.”

“Under the impression that they scarcely furnish Christian cheer of mind or body to the multitude,” returned the gentleman, “a few of us are endeavouring to raise a fund to buy the Poor some meat and drink, and means of warmth. We choose this time, because it is a time, of all others, when Want is keenly felt, and Abundance rejoices. What shall I put you down for?”

“Nothing,” Scrooge replied.

“You wish to be anonymous?”

“I wish to be left alone,” said Scrooge. “Since you ask me what I wish, gentlemen, that is my answer. I don't make merry myself at Christmas, and I can't afford to make idle people merry. I help to support the establishments I have mentioned—they cost enough; and those who are badly off must go there.”

“Many can't go there; and many would rather die.”

“If they would rather die,” said Scrooge, “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population. You have just met a gentleman in the passage, I think, who has a different opinion. His liberality is quite at your service, and quite enough, I daresay, for himself and you too. Good afternoon, gentlemen!”

The portly gentlemen looked at one another, and at Scrooge, who had already taken up his pen and bent himself to his book with the air of a man who considered the interview at an end, and withdrew with what grace they might. Scrooge resumed his labours with an improved opinion of himself, which was saying a great deal in Scrooge's case, for his opinion of himself was seldom a low one; and yet there was something in the chink of his nephew's money, still ringing pleasantly and reproachfully in his ears, that kept his humour from being completely facetious. He added a column twice over, and made an error in the total both times; a circumstance which would have amazed him at any other season of the year, and which he set down, very properly, to the fog.

The fog and the darkness thickened as the afternoon went on, so that people ran about with flaring links, proffering their services to go before horses in carriages, and conduct them on their way. The ancient tower of a church, whose gruff old bell was always peeping slily down at Scrooge out of a Gothic window in the wall, became invisible, and struck the hours and quarters in the clouds, with tremulous vibrations afterwards, as if its teeth were chattering in its frozen head up there. The cold became intense. In the main street, at the corner of the court, some labourers were repairing the gas-pipes, and had lighted a great fire in a brazier, round which a party of ragged men and boys were gathered, warming their hands and winking their eyes before the blaze in rapture. The brightness of the shops, where holly-sprigs and berries crackled in the lamp-heat of the windows, made the pale faces ruddy as they passed. Poulterers' and grocers' trades became a splendid joke, a glorious pageant, with which it was next to impossible to believe that such dull principles as bargain and sale had anything to do.

A small boy, with a scant young nose gnawed and mumbled by the hungry cold, stooped down at the keyhole of the counting-house to regale Scrooge with a Christmas carol; but at the first faint sounds of “God bless you, merry gentleman,” Scrooge seized the ruler with such energy of action that the singer fled in terror, leaving the keyhole to the fog, and to even more congenial frost.

At length the hour of shutting up arrived. With an ill-will Scrooge dismounted from his stool, and tacitly admitted the fact to the expectant clerk in the Tank, who instantly snuffed his candle out, and put his hat on.

“You'll want all day to-morrow, I suppose?” said Scrooge.

“If quite convenient, sir.”

“It's not convenient,” said Scrooge, “and it's not fair. If I was to stop half-a-crown for it, you'd think yourself ill-used, I'll be bound?”

The clerk smiled faintly.

“And yet,” said Scrooge, “you don't think me ill-used, when I pay a day's wages for no work. A poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December! But I suppose you must have the whole day. Be here all the earlier next morning.”

The clerk promised that he would. As he wound his white comforter about his throat (for he boasted no great-coat), he ventured, with a timidity that made his voice very small indeed, to say that he was glad—he hoped he might be forgiven for saying so—to hear that Mr. Scrooge was to dine with his nephew to-morrow.

“You heard a great deal more than was intended for you, then,” said Scrooge. “Hold your tongue about it, if you value your situation. It's a business engagement, and nothing else.”

“I'm sure it'll do you good, sir,” said the clerk, and vanished down the court with the long ends of his comforter dangling below his waist, going off at last down a slide on Cornhill, at the end of a lane of boys, twenty times, in honour of its being Christmas Eve, and then running home to Camden Town as hard as he could pelt, to play at blindman's-buff.

Scrooge walked out with a growl. The office was closed in a twinkling behind him. He had taken perhaps a dozen paces in the direction of his usual melancholy tavern, when a wine merchant's window, blazing cheerfully through the fog with pyramids of bottles and decanters, stopped him short. It came into his mind—who can tell how such unwelcome ideas force themselves into minds that are determined to receive nothing?—that a man does not go to another man's house at Christmas, and eat another man's goose, and drink another man's health, entirely empty-handed, without people remarking upon it behind his back. It was not generosity that troubled Scrooge. It was the fear of being thought mean by people whose good opinion he professed to despise; which is often the same hard master, under a different name.

He went into the shop, where a sleek shopman, with a waistcoat that seemed to have been warmed at the same fire as his ruddy face, was polishing a glass by the counter and humming the fag-end of a tune.

“I want a bottle of port,” said Scrooge. “For to-morrow.”

“For to-morrow, sir! For Christmas Day! Then we must have something particular. Here is a wine now—”

“I didn't say particular,” said Scrooge. “I said a bottle. What is the cheapest in the shop?”

The shopman ceased to hum. He brought forth, one after another, sundry bottles of improving aspect and increasing recommendation, and laid them on the counter with the air of a man displaying so many virtues in a row. Scrooge rejected them all, with increasing firmness. At last a small dusty bottle was produced from a remote bin, whose label had seen better days, and whose contents, according to the shopman, with a visible reluctance to part with his integrity together with his wine, were “sound enough, sir; sound enough for ordinary purposes.”

“Ordinary purposes will do,” said Scrooge. “My nephew is not a judge of wine. He would drink vinegar, I believe, and call it Christmas, if there was company enough to clink glasses with.”

The bottle was wrapped in brown paper, corked, sealed, and entered; but not, if Scrooge could have helped it, paid for at a farthing beyond its price. He carried it under his arm to the tavern, where he took his melancholy dinner as usual, and, having read all the newspapers and beguiled the rest of the evening with his banker's-book, set it down beside his plate like a poor relation that had followed him, uninvited, out of the fog.

“What is that, Mr. Scrooge?” said the waiter, who knew his habits and his humours, and was curious in spite of both.

“A Christmas present,” said Scrooge, “for a nephew. A foolish boy, who has married on nothing, and keeps Christmas on less. It will teach him the value of good wine.”

“He'll be glad to see you, sir, I'm sure,” said the waiter.

“He'll be glad to see my money spent,” said Scrooge. “There's a difference. Bring me the bill.”

Having paid it, to the last fraction that was due, and not a fraction more, he took the bottle and went home to bed. He lived in chambers which had once belonged to his deceased partner. They were a gloomy suite of rooms, in a lowering pile of building up a yard, where it had so little business to be that one could scarcely help fancying it must have run there when it was a young house, playing at hide-and-seek with other houses, and forgotten the way out again. It was old enough now, and dreary enough, for nobody lived in it but Scrooge, the other rooms being all let out as offices.

The yard was so dark that even Scrooge, who knew its every stone, was fain to grope with his hands. The fog and frost so hung about the black old gateway of the house that it seemed as if the Genius of the Weather sat in mournful meditation on the threshold.

Now, it is a fact that there was nothing at all particular about the knocker on the door, except that it was very large. It is also a fact that Scrooge had seen it, night and morning, during his whole residence in that place; also that Scrooge had as little of what is called fancy about him as any man in the city of London, even including—which is a bold word—the corporation, aldermen, and livery. Let it also be borne in mind that Scrooge had not bestowed one thought on Marley, since his last mention of his seven years' dead partner that afternoon, unless the recollection of his nephew's foolish gift at the counting-house door be counted for a thought about liberality, which is a very different matter. And then let any man explain to me, if he can, how it happened that Scrooge, having his key in the lock of the door, saw in the knocker, without its undergoing any intermediate process of change—not a knocker, but Marley's face.

Marley's face. It was not in impenetrable shadow, as the other objects in the yard were, but had a dismal light about it, like a bad lobster in a dark cellar. It was not angry or ferocious, but looked at Scrooge as Marley used to look, with ghostly spectacles turned up on its ghostly forehead. The hair was curiously stirred, as if by breath or hot air; and, though the eyes were wide open, they were perfectly motionless. That, and its livid colour, made it horrible; but its horror seemed to be in spite of the face, and beyond its control, rather than a part of its own expression.

As Scrooge looked fixedly at this phenomenon, it was a knocker again.

To say that he was not startled, or that his blood was not conscious of a terrible sensation to which it had been a stranger from infancy, would be untrue. But he put his hand upon the key he had relinquished, turned it sturdily, put the bottle of port more firmly under his arm, walked in, and lighted his candle.

He did pause, with a moment's irresolution, before he shut the door; and he did look cautiously behind it first, as if he half expected to be terrified with the sight of Marley's pigtail sticking out into the hall. But there was nothing on the back of the door except the screws and nuts that held the knocker on, so he said, “Pooh, pooh!” and closed it with a bang.

The sound resounded through the house like thunder. Every room above, and every cask in the wine-merchant's cellars below, appeared to have a separate peal of echoes of its own. Scrooge was not a man to be frightened by echoes. He fastened the door, and walked across the hall, and up the stairs, slowly too, trimming his candle as he went, and clasping the brown-paper parcel as if it had been a cash-box.

Up Scrooge went, not caring a button for that. Darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it. But before he shut his heavy door, he walked through his rooms to see that all was right. He had just enough recollection of the face to desire to do that. Sitting-room, bedroom, lumber-room. All as they should be. Nobody under the table, nobody under the sofa; a small fire in the grate; spoon and basin ready; and the little saucepan of gruel (Scrooge had a cold in his head) upon the hob. Nobody under the bed; nobody in the closet; nobody in his dressing-gown, which was hanging up in a suspicious attitude against the wall.

Quite satisfied, he closed his door, and locked himself in; double-locked himself in, which was not his custom. He set the port upon the table, with a precautionary look at the seal, as if even a shadow might be expected to broach it; took off his cravat; put on his dressing-gown and slippers and his nightcap; and sat down before the fire to take his gruel.

It was a very low fire indeed; nothing on such a bitter night. He was obliged to sit close to it and brood over it, before he could extract the least sensation of warmth from such a handful of fuel. The fireplace was an old one, built by some Dutch merchant long ago, and paved all round with quaint Dutch tiles, designed to illustrate the Scriptures; and yet that face of Marley, seven years dead, came like the ancient Prophet's rod, and swallowed up the whole. If each smooth tile had been a blank at first, with power to shape some picture on its surface from the disjointed fragments of his thoughts, there would have been a copy of old Marley's head on every one.

“Humbug!” said Scrooge, and walked across the room.

After several turns, he sat down again. As he threw his head back in the chair, his glance happened to rest upon a bell, a disused bell that hung in the room, and communicated for some purpose now forgotten with a chamber in the highest story of the building. It was with great astonishment, and with a strange, inexplicable dread, that, as he looked, he saw this bell begin to swing. It swung so softly in the outset that it scarcely made a sound; but soon it rang out loudly, and so did every bell in the house.

This might have lasted half a minute, or a minute, but it seemed an hour. The bells ceased as they had begun, together. They were succeeded by a clanking noise, deep down below, as if some person were dragging a heavy chain over the casks in the wine-merchant's cellar. Scrooge then remembered to have heard that ghosts in haunted houses were described as dragging chains.

The cellar-door flew open with a booming sound, and then he heard the noise much louder, on the floors below; then coming up the stairs; then coming straight towards his door.

“It's humbug still!” said Scrooge. “I won't believe it.”

His colour changed, though, when, without a pause, it came on through the heavy door and passed into the room before his eyes. Upon its coming in, the dying flame leaped up, as though it cried, “I know him; Marley's Ghost!” and fell again.

The same face: the very same. Marley in his pigtail, usual waistcoat, tights and boots; the tassels on the latter bristling, like his pigtail, and his coat-skirts, and the hair upon his head. The chain he drew was clasped about his middle. It was long, and wound about him like a tail; and it was made (for Scrooge observed it closely) of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel. His body was transparent, so that Scrooge, observing him, and looking through his waistcoat, could see the two buttons on his coat behind. The brown-paper bottle upon the table seemed, by a strange kind of fellowship, to be the only object in the room besides Scrooge himself that was altogether solid.

Scrooge had often heard it said that Marley had no bowels, but he had never believed it until now. No, nor did he believe it even now. Though he looked the phantom through and through, and saw it standing before him; though he felt the chilling influence of its death-cold eyes, and marked the very texture of the folded kerchief bound about its head and chin, which wrapper he had not observed before; he was still incredulous, and fought against his senses.

“How now!” said Scrooge, caustic and cold as ever. “What do you want with me?”

“Much!”—Marley's voice, no doubt about it.

“Who are you?”

“Ask me who I was.”

“Who were you, then?” said Scrooge, raising his voice. “You're particular, for a shade.”

“In life I was your partner, Jacob Marley.”

“Can you—can you sit down?” asked Scrooge, looking doubtfully at him.

“I can.”

“Do it, then.”

The ghost sat down on the opposite side of the fireplace, as if he were quite used to it, and the chain made a dismal music among the fender-irons.

“You don't believe in me,” observed the Ghost.

“I don't,” said Scrooge.

“What evidence would you have of my reality beyond that of your senses?”

“I don't know,” said Scrooge.

“Why do you doubt your senses?”

“Because,” said Scrooge, “a little thing affects them. A slight disorder of the stomach makes them cheats. You may be an undigested bit of beef, a blot of mustard, a crumb of cheese, a fragment of an underdone potato. There's more of gravy than of grave about you, whatever you are!”

Scrooge tried to be smart, as a means of distracting his own attention and keeping down his terror; for the spectre's voice disturbed the very marrow in his bones. There was something very awful, too, in the spectre's being provided with an infernal atmosphere of its own. Scrooge could not feel it himself, but this was clearly the case; for though the Ghost sat perfectly motionless, its hair, and skirts, and tassels were still agitated, as by the hot vapour from an oven.

“Well!” returned Scrooge, endeavouring to look at anything but those fixed glazed eyes, and lighting, in his extremity, upon the parcel by the gruel-basin. “I have my engagements. I dine out to-morrow. With my nephew. A family dinner, at four o'clock precisely. If you are a spirit of business, you'll not keep a man from keeping his engagements.”

The Ghost turned its head slowly towards the bottle, and the brown paper rustled of itself in the unnatural air.

“You have promised your body to a feast, Ebenezer,” it said. “See that your spirit is not left standing at the door.”

“I go because it's cheap,” said Scrooge, with a hard defiance born of fright. “I go because a free dinner is not to be refused in these hard times. There is no sentiment in it. Don't mistake me.”

“I made no mistake in life,” returned the Ghost, “except the mistake of all my life. I too reckoned what a thing cost, and never what it was worth. I too kept my spirit within our counting-house, and called the narrowness of it wisdom.”

At this the spirit raised a frightful cry, and shook its chain with such a dismal and appalling noise that Scrooge held on tight to his chair, to save himself from falling in a swoon. But how much greater was his horror, when the phantom, taking off the bandage round its head, as if it were too warm to wear indoors, suffered its lower jaw to drop down upon its breast!

Scrooge fell upon his knees, and clasped his hands before his face.

“Mercy!” he said. “Dreadful apparition, why do you trouble me?”

“Man of the worldly mind!” replied the Ghost. “Do you believe in me or not?”

“I do,” said Scrooge. “I must. But why do spirits walk the earth, and why do they come to me?”

“It is required of every man,” the Ghost returned, “that the spirit within him should walk abroad among his fellow-men, and travel far and wide; and if that spirit goes not forth in life, it is condemned to do so after death. It is doomed to wander through the world—oh, woe is me!—and witness what it cannot share, but might have shared on earth, and turned to happiness!”

Again the spectre raised a cry, and shook its chain and wrung its shadowy hands.

“You are fettered,” said Scrooge, trembling. “Tell me why.”

“I wear the chain I forged in life,” replied the Ghost. “I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it. Is its pattern strange to you? Or would you know the weight and length of the strong coil you bear yourself? It was full as heavy and as long as this, seven Christmas Eves ago. You have laboured on it since. It is a ponderous chain!”

Scrooge glanced about him on the floor, in the expectation of finding himself surrounded by some fifty or sixty fathoms of iron cable; but he could see nothing, except that the little bottle, for aught he knew, might have been the first link of another sort of forging, and looked unaccountably accusing in its brown paper.

“Jacob,” he said imploringly, “old Jacob Marley, tell me more. Speak comfort to me, Jacob!”

“I have none to give,” the Ghost replied. “It comes from other regions, Ebenezer Scrooge, and is conveyed by other ministers, to other kinds of men. Nor can I tell you what I would. A very little more is all permitted to me. I cannot rest, I cannot stay, I cannot linger anywhere. My spirit never walked beyond our counting-house—mark me!—in life my spirit never roved beyond the narrow limits of our money-changing hole; and weary journeys lie before me!”

“You must have been very slow about it, Jacob,” Scrooge observed, in a business-like manner, though with humility and deference, and still upon his knees.

“Slow!” the Ghost repeated.

“Seven years dead,” mused Scrooge, “and travelling all the time.”

“The whole time,” said the Ghost. “No rest, no peace. Incessant torture of remorse.”

“Oh! captive, bound, and double-ironed,” cried the phantom, after another pause, in which Scrooge dared not lift his eyes, “not to know that any Christian spirit working kindly in its little sphere, whatever it may be, will find its mortal life too short for its vast means of usefulness! Not to know that no space of regret can make amends for one life's opportunity misused! Yet such was I! Oh, such was I!”

“But you were always a good man of business, Jacob,” faltered Scrooge, who now began to apply this to himself.

“Business!” cried the Ghost, wringing its hands again. “Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence were, all, my business. The dealings of my trade were but a drop of water in the comprehensive ocean of my business!”

It held up its chain at arm's length, as if that were the cause of all its unavailing grief, and flung it heavily upon the ground again.

“At this time of the rolling year,” the spectre said, “I suffer most. Why did I walk through crowds of fellow-beings with my eyes turned down, and never raise them to that blessed Star which led the Wise Men to a poor abode? Were there no poor homes to which its light would have conducted me!”

Scrooge was very much dismayed to hear the spectre going on at this rate, and began to quake exceedingly.

“Hear me!” cried the Ghost. “My time is nearly gone.”

“I will,” said Scrooge. “But don't be hard upon me! Don't be flowery, Jacob! Pray!”

“How it is that I appear before you in a shape that you can see, I may not tell. I have sat invisible beside you many and many a day.”

That was not an agreeable idea. Scrooge shivered, and wiped the perspiration from his brow.

“That is no light part of my penance,” pursued the Ghost. “I am here to-night to warn you that you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate. A chance and hope of my procuring, Ebenezer.”

“You were always a good friend to me,” said Scrooge. “Thank'ee!”

“You have taken your nephew's hand this day,” said the Ghost. “Take care that it prove not the merest bargain of your life. A door may be opened by the hand, and yet the man may stand shivering on the threshold, and call it entering in.”

“I told you,” said Scrooge, “I go for the dinner.”

“Go, then,” said the Ghost; “and mark what hunger is, and what feeding is. But alone, that will not save you.”

“You will be haunted,” resumed the Ghost, “by Three Spirits.”

Scrooge's countenance fell almost as low as the Ghost's had done.

“Is that the chance and hope you mentioned, Jacob?” he demanded, in a faltering voice.

“It is.”

“I—I think I'd rather not,” said Scrooge.

“Without their visits,” said the Ghost, “you cannot hope to shun the path I tread. Expect the first to-morrow, when the bell tolls One.”

“To-morrow!” said Scrooge. “But to-morrow is Christmas Day, and I am engaged to dine—”

“Expect the first to-morrow,” said the Ghost, “when the bell tolls One. The dinner is between this night and then. Keep it with your eyes open. Expect the second on the next night at the same hour. The third upon the next night, when the last stroke of Twelve has ceased to vibrate. Look to see me no more; and look that, for your own sake, you remember what has passed between us.”

When it had said these words, the spectre took its wrapper from the table, and bound it round its head as before. Scrooge knew this by the smart sound its teeth made when the jaws were brought together by the bandage. He ventured to raise his eyes again, and found his supernatural visitor confronting him in an erect attitude, with its chain wound over and about its arm. The apparition walked backward from him; and at every step it took, the window raised itself a little, so that when the spectre reached it, it was wide open.

It beckoned Scrooge to approach, which he did. When they were within two paces of each other, Marley's Ghost held up its hand, warning him to come no nearer. Scrooge stopped, not so much in obedience as in surprise and fear; for, on the raising of the hand, he became sensible of confused noises in the air, incoherent sounds of lamentation and regret, wailings inexpressibly sorrowful and self-accusatory. The spectre, after listening for a moment, joined in the mournful dirge, and floated out upon the bleak, dark night.

Scrooge followed to the window, desperate in his curiosity, and looked out. The air was filled with phantoms, wandering hither and thither in restless haste, and moaning as they went. Every one of them wore chains like Marley's Ghost; some few were linked together; none were free. Many had been personally known to Scrooge in their lives. He had been quite familiar with one old ghost in a white waistcoat, with a monstrous iron safe attached to its ankle, who cried piteously at being unable to assist a wretched woman with an infant, whom it saw below upon a door-step. The misery with them all was, clearly, that they sought to interfere, for good, in human matters, and had lost the power for ever.

Whether these creatures faded into mist, or mist enshrouded them, he could not tell. But they and their spirit voices faded together, and the night became as it had been when he walked home.

Scrooge closed the window, and examined the door by which the Ghost had entered. It was double-locked, as he had locked it with his own hands, and the bolts were undisturbed. He tried to say “Humbug!” but stopped at the first syllable, and, looking at the little bottle on the table, found that his hand trembled when he reached to move it farther from the edge. Being, from the emotion he had undergone, or the fatigues of the day, or his glimpse of the Invisible World, or the dull conversation of the Ghost, or the lateness of the hour, much in need of repose, he went straight to bed, without undressing, and fell asleep upon the instant.

***

He awoke on Christmas morning with the church bells ringing as if they had gone mad with joy, and with a firm resolution, the first thing he did, to send a boy (if a boy could be found on Christmas Day, which was doubtful) with a note to his nephew, pleading a cold, a headache, the state of the weather, and every other convenient infirmity that might occur to a man of business desirous of breaking an engagement without exactly breaking his word. But there was no boy. There never is a boy in Scrooge's chambers, at any hour, for any purpose. He got up, shaved himself with a razor that seemed to object to the proceeding, dressed in his Sunday waistcoat (which fitted him as closely as his opinions), and stood for a long time before the bottle, as if it had been a witness summoned against him.

“If I don't go,” said Scrooge, addressing the brown paper, “he'll come here. He'll come here with that wife of his, and carols, and God bless you's, and make the place uninhabitable. I may as well have the goose for my pains. Besides, Jacob—”

He stopped. He had not meant to speak that name aloud, in the broad daylight, with the bells ringing. It sounded as if the room disapproved of it.

By the time he had buttoned his greatcoat to the chin, and taken the bottle once more under his arm, the stern logic of his own bargain had him fast. He had promised; promises, in Scrooges's creed, were debts; and debts, whether to be paid or received, were not things to be trifled with. He went down the dark staircase, not unaware that he carried, in addition to a very indifferent bottle of port, the uncomfortable recollection of a chain that clanked in an empty room, and of certain words about standing on a threshold which he was quite unable to get rid of by calling them humbug.

The streets were quieter than on the previous evening, but with a deeper and more settled gladness. There was a smell of cooking in the air, even in the poorest courts; a savour of goose and pudding, issuing from a hundred invisible kitchens, and mingling with the sharp frost in a manner that made the hungry poorer and the comfortable hungrier. People were going to church in their best clothes, with their faces washed very clean, and their children scrubbed into a state of unnatural and protesting brightness. Others carried covered dishes to the bakers', and came back with them steaming, under cloths, as if they bore some small and precious volcano in triumph through the streets. Scrooge eyed them all with disfavour, and considered that Christmas Day, viewed from the pavement, was a conspiracy of smells against a man who had breakfasted upon gruel.

His nephew's house was not a large one—Scrooge had known that before, and had set it down, very correctly, as one of the consequences of marrying for love—but it had a sprig of holly over the door, and windows so bright with firelight and candlelight that they seemed to be laughing at the winter afternoon before the afternoon was well begun. As Scrooge came up the steps, with the bottle under his arm and his most forbidding countenance screwed up to receive civility without returning it, the door was flung open by his nephew himself, in his shirt-sleeves and an apron, with his face flushed from the kitchen fire, and a carving-knife (hastily laid down, but not so hastily as to prevent its existence from being evident) somewhere in the immediate neighbourhood.

“Uncle!” cried he. “My dear uncle! Come in, come in! You are punctual as the Bank.”

“I said four,” said Scrooge. “It is four.”

“So it is, and you are as good as your word, which is more than Christmas usually gets credit for. Give me your hat. Give me your coat. Susan! Here's my uncle!”

A young wife came forward out of the warm parlour; not a grand lady, nor a beauty in the Almanack sense of the word, but a pleasant, rosy, clear-eyed creature, with such a welcoming manner that Scrooge, who had come armed at all points against affection, felt his weapons to be unaccountably heavy. There were guests besides: a cheerful friend of his nephew's, with a laugh that was too large for the room and had to be let out in instalments; the wife's sister, a plump, good-humoured girl, who seemed to consider the whole world as a pudding that had turned out well; a maiden aunt of somebody's, very deaf, very sharp-eyed, and possessed of a miraculous faculty for hearing anything that was said about money; and one or two more, whose names Scrooge did not catch, and did not ask for.

“This is my uncle Scrooge,” said his nephew, presenting him as if he had been a prize ox at Smithfield, “who has honoured us at last. Uncle, you know everybody by wishing them well, which is the best introduction at Christmas.”

“I know nobody,” said Scrooge, “and I wish—hem!—I wish you a—a—”

He stuck fast. The word “merry” seemed to rise into his throat and refuse to come any farther, like a plum that was too large for the pudding.

“The same to you, sir, I'm sure,” said the wife, supplying the deficiency so neatly that it hardly showed. “Will you have a glass of something warm before dinner? We have been keeping a place by the fire for you this half-hour.”

“Keeping a place by the fire” was, in Scrooge's vocabulary, waste of coals; but he submitted to be led to the chair, and even accepted, though with a suspicious glance at its dimensions, a footstool that the plump sister placed for him as if she had been laying a small offering on an altar. The bottle he produced with an air of great unwillingness, setting it down upon the table as if he parted with it under protest.

“I have brought this,” said he. “It's port. I don't know that it's good. I was not going to ruin myself in wine for a fancy dinner.”

“It is exactly what we wanted,” said his nephew's wife, with a gravity that would have done credit to a duchess receiving a service of plate. “We were lamenting, not five minutes ago, that we had no port fit to put before a connoisseur. Weren't we?”

An unanimous and entirely shameless assent went round the room. The cheerful friend declared that the shape of the bottle promised everything; the plump sister, who knew no more of port than of Sanscrit, pronounced the seal to be “quite beautiful.” Scrooge, who understood flattery when it was laid on with a trowel, and liked it no better for understanding it, saw that he was being humoured, and was angry; and yet there was something in the ready good-nature with which these poor people took his sour gift and turned it sweet, that made his anger sit uneasily upon him.

The dinner came in. It was not a Lord Mayor's dinner; it was not a dinner to make the poulterers jealous, or to cause grocers to retire from business in despair. The goose was a modest goose, and had evidently been acquainted with economy in its lifetime; the apple-sauce was in a small tureen, the mashed potatoes in a smaller; the pudding, when it made its appearance, blazing in a spirit that seemed to have been borrowed for the occasion, was received with a shout that a much larger pudding might have envied. But there was enough, and to spare; and what is more (a circumstance which Scrooge had never taken into his calculations upon the subject of dinner before), there was more than enough, because nobody counted whether there was enough. His nephew carved with a flourish that supplied the want of gravy in at least three places, and his nephew's wife dispensed the vegetables as if they had been the revenues of a kingdom, established for the sole purpose of giving everybody a share.

Scrooge ate. He could not help eating. He began, indeed, with a determination to find fault with everything, and expressed himself with freedom upon the goose (“tough”), the sauce (“sharp”), and the potatoes (“lumpy”); but the company received his criticisms with such entire good-humour, and his nephew answered them with such hearty laughter, and his plate was replenished so promptly whenever it became empty, that he insensibly fell into the mechanical process of a man who is enjoying his dinner and does not intend to own it.

“You keep a cook, I suppose?” said he to his nephew's wife, as a forced contribution to conversation.

“We keep Susan,” said she, “three days in the week, and ourselves the other four. But to-day Susan has done wonders, hasn't she, uncle?”

“Don't call me uncle,” said Scrooge. “I am not used to it.”

“I shall call you uncle all the same,” she returned, smiling; “because you are.”

Scrooge was silent. There is no argument known to man, or at least to Scrooge, against a fact of that kind, when it is stated by a person who has just given him a second helping of pudding.

“You married on very little,” he said to his nephew, reverting to the one topic upon which he felt himself strong.

“On very little indeed,” said his nephew, “except good-humour; and that's better than a balance at the banker's, as long as it lasts.”

“If it flags—” began Scrooge.

“Why, then, uncle, we must make it up with love, which is a capital that increases the more you spend it. Isn't that your business doctrine?”

“Don't quote me against myself,” said Scrooge; “it's not fair. I never said anything of the kind.”

“No,” said his nephew, quietly. “But I think you feel it sometimes, for all that.”

The maiden aunt, who had been deaf to the whole preceding conversation, chose this precise moment to become miraculously audible, and inquired, in a high and penetrating voice, whether Mr. Scrooge was in the Funds; to which the plump sister replied, in an equally penetrating whisper which was heard in the kitchen, that Mr. Scrooge was the Funds. A general laugh ensued, in which Scrooge, to his own unspeakable astonishment, very nearly joined. He converted it, by a great effort, into a cough; but the plump sister, who caught the twinkle before he could extinguish it, clapped her hands and declared that uncle had laughed; and, this being taken up by the cheerful friend, and echoed by his nephew with a delight quite out of proportion to the merit of the joke, Scrooge was betrayed into the ghost of a smile before he could prevent it.

When the cloth was drawn, and the port—Scrooge's port—was set upon the table with a reverence that made him ashamed of knowing how little it had cost, there was a pause, as if some customary grace were expected. His nephew rose. His face was graver than Scrooge had ever seen it, under all its cheerfulness, though the cheerfulness was still there, shining through, like firelight through a lattice.

He lifted his glass, and looked, not round the table only, but directly, and with a sort of affectionate defiance, at Scrooge himself; and Scrooge, who had braced his whole soul to endure a speech about Christmas, felt himself unaccountably discomposed by being looked at with kindness by a man whom he had spent twenty years in trying to disappoint.

“To my uncle,” said his nephew. “A merry Christmas and a happy New Year to him, whatever he thinks of us for wishing it. He has given us a great deal of merriment to-day, without knowing it, perhaps; but he has given us, what is better, the pleasure of having him among us. Here's to him, and to all of us, and to everybody who is not here to be toasted in person!”

They drank. They drank with a will; even the maiden aunt, who required the toast to be explained to her twice, and then drank to “the Funds,” contributed her mite of goodwill. Scrooge sat with his glass untasted in his hand. He had intended to say “Humbug” at the proper moment, by way of clearing his conscience and maintaining his character; but the word had gone somewhere out of the room, and left him in the lurch. He set the glass down again, very carefully, as if it had been made of something more brittle than crockery.

“Thank you,” said Scrooge, at last, in a voice so unlike his own that his nephew stared. “I am obliged to you. It's more than I've deserved at your hands, I daresay. Ahem! You are a foolish fellow, but you're—you're not a bad one.”

This was considered, by the whole company, as an outburst of tenderness so remarkable that it required a round of applause to do it justice; during which Scrooge recovered himself, and assumed an aspect of the deepest severity, as a man who has let the enemy into the citadel and is determined, at all events, to keep them out of the powder-magazine.

After dinner there was music. The plump sister played the harp—not with science, perhaps, but with a will, and with a knowledge of all the tunes that everybody liked; the cheerful friend sang a song that was more remarkable for its chorus than its melody, into which everybody entered, including (at a respectful distance, and under his breath) the foot of Scrooge against the leg of the table. It was beaten time upon the floor, quite unconsciously, until he discovered it in the act and withdrew it hastily, as if it had been a clerk caught warming himself at the candle.

Then there were games. Blindman's-buff was proposed, with all the ardour that distinguishes people who are quite sure of not being made ridiculous by it themselves; but Scrooge, being requested to take his turn in the handkerchief, declined with great positiveness, and retired into the post of spectator by the fire, from which eminence he surveyed the proceedings with the air of a magistrate who disapproves of the sport, but will not interfere unless the furniture suffers. His nephew's wife, blindfolded, caught the cheerful friend by the button-hole and guessed him on the instant, to the great delight of the company; the plump sister ran against the maiden aunt, and was forgiven before she was hurt; his nephew himself, in dodging round the table, came within an inch of upsetting Scrooge's chair, and begged his pardon with a “Whoa, uncle!” that set them all laughing again.

Scrooge bore it for half-an-hour; for three-quarters; for longer, indeed, than he afterwards would allow to himself in his own private reckonings upon the subject. But when a pause came in the game, and he rose from his chair, saying that it was time for an old man to be thinking of his bed (which was a fiction; he never thought of his bed until he fell into it), his nephew pressed him to stay, his nephew's wife pressed him, the company pressed him, with such a chorus of “Oh, don't go yet, uncle!” and “One game, only one game!” that he was fain to escape, abruptly and almost rudely, into the little hall, to fetch his own hat and greatcoat, rather than trust them to hands that might detain him by the button-hole.

The hall was cold after the parlour, and dark, except for a thin line of light under the dining-room door. As Scrooge stood there, fumbling, in his nervousness, with the buttons of his coat, the game within was hushed, and he heard—not that he listened, for Scrooge was not a listener at keyholes, and would have told you so with indignation—the voice of the cheerful friend, lowered, but not so low as it ought to have been.

“He's a comical old fellow,” said the voice, “if one could only get at the comedy of him. He sat at dinner like a milestone at a wedding. Upon my word, I don't think he'd have passed the pudding if the poor had had a prior claim to it. Decrease the surplus population, indeed!”

Scrooge's hand stopped upon the third button.

“Don't laugh at him,” said his nephew. Scrooge knew that voice, even through the door, with its laugh gone out of it. “Don't laugh at him; at least, not in that way. His offences carry their own punishment, and I have nothing to say against him. He is rich, and we are poor; but who suffers by his ill whims? Himself, always. Here he is, discontented with us all, and discontented with himself most of all, I believe; and if he loses a little pleasure by it—why, there are not many people who would envy him the bargain. I am sorry for him. I couldn't be angry with him if I tried. Who suffers? Himself, always.”

There was a short silence. Then his nephew's wife spoke, gently, but with a spirit of her own.

“He came,” she said, “which is more than I expected; and he has eaten his dinner like a Christian, which is more than he expected himself, I think. Let us be content with so much for once, and not ask the poor old gentleman to turn merry all in a moment, like a pancake.”

Scrooge did not hear the laugh that followed. He had got his coat buttoned wrong, which was a thing that had not happened to him for thirty years, and he did not perceive it. He opened the street door very softly, and shut it after him without calling out so much as a good-night; and stood for a full minute on the steps outside, in the fog, with his hat in his hand, as if he had forgotten which way his own house lay.

The night had come down while they were at table. The shops were shut, the streets were muffled, and here and there a late carol-singer, or a link-boy with his torch burned down to a red eye in the mist, went by like a spirit that had lost its way and did not much care about finding it. On a doorstep, not twenty paces from his nephew's house, a woman sat with a child asleep against her breast, wrapped in a shawl that was more hole than shawl, waiting—for what, Scrooge did not stop to ask—until the world should be pleased to take some notice of her. He passed her, as he had passed a thousand such in his life, with the usual tightening of his lips and quickening of his step; and had got as far as the corner when a sound behind him made him turn his head. It was only the boy singer, whom he had driven from his keyhole yesterday—no, it could not be the same boy; all such boys are the same boy to Scrooge—striking up, very small and hoarse, round the corner of the court, “God bless you, merry gentleman.” The woman on the doorstep lifted her face at the sound, not as if the blessing were for her, but as if she were glad that it was for anybody.

Scrooge stood still. The fog was in his throat, or something was. The chain he had heard in his own room clanked again, somewhere between his conscience and his memory; and the words of his nephew, spoken through a shut door to people who did not know he heard them—“Who suffers? Himself, always”—came back upon him with a force that mere anger, or mere contempt, had never been able to command. He had been pitied in that warm little room, pitied by the very man he had come to confute; and he found, to his unspeakable confusion, that pity was a coin he did not know how to refuse, and could not bear to keep.

The corner was gained; his own dark way home lay straight before him; the lit windows of his nephew's house were already blurred to two dim yellow squares in the mist. What he did next, he did so quickly, and with such a vehement determination not to give himself time to reconsider it, that he was half-way back before he knew that his feet had turned. Up the familiar steps he went, with his greatcoat still buttoned crooked, and the warmth of the firelight coming out to meet him through the fanlight over the door.

From within came the scrape of a chair, the sudden hush of the game as it broke off in the middle, and his nephew's voice, nearer than the rest, saying something that Scrooge could not distinguish. He did not wait to distinguish it. He lifted the knocker, and let it fall, once, sharply; and then stood in the fog, with his hat in his hands and the light falling on his white hair, waiting to be let in.

chapter.chapter:
He might have spoken, but I did not hear; one hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me, and I believe I should have escaped and rushed downstairs had not a thought, more powerful even than horror, arrested my steps. He knew nothing of the world into which I had summoned him; he could not name the cold that shook his vast frame, nor ask for the aid he sought. If I fled from him in the first hour of his life, I should not merely abandon a monster—I should make him one by abandonment, and send misery, ignorant and gigantic, to find its own path among men.

I remained, therefore, though my heart beat so violently that I feared its sound alone would betray me. Slowly, and with an effort greater than any I had exerted in the construction of that form, I raised my hand towards his. His fingers closed round it; they were cold, and of a magnitude that filled me with renewed affright, yet their pressure was uncertain rather than violent, as if he feared to injure the thing he touched. I drew him from beside the bed, speaking in the low tones one uses to a child awakened by dreams. "Come," I said; "you suffer. Come with me."

He stooped beneath the doorway and followed, his steps unsteady, his watery eyes fixed upon me with an expression I dared not interpret. In the adjoining chamber the instruments of my fatal work still lay scattered around; the table on which he had lain lifeless stood in the centre, and for an instant the sight nearly overcame the resolution I had formed. I turned from it and made him sit upon the floor before the stove, for no chair could have borne his proportions without groaning beneath them. With hands that trembled so that I could scarcely strike a light, I kindled the fire; then I brought water in a cup and held it to his lips.

At first he drew back, ignorant of my purpose; but thirst soon instructed him. He drank awkwardly, the water running from the corners of his mouth, while I supported the cup lest it should fall from his enormous hand. I softened bread in the remainder and fed him as one feeds an infant, morsel by morsel, until the violence of his shivering began to abate. Then I took my own cloak from its peg and drew it about his shoulders, fastening the clasp beneath his chin. The garment, ample upon me, scarcely covered his breast, yet he looked down at it and touched the wool with a slow wonder.

"Water," I said, pointing to the cup. "Fire. Bread." I repeated the words, not expecting an answer, but because silence beside him was more terrible than speech. His lips moved; some inarticulate sound issued, harsh and broken, and that grin which had filled me with terror appeared again upon his cheeks. I perceived then, with a sensation for which I can find no name, that it might be his untaught attempt to answer kindness in the only expression he had yet seen upon a human face.

I watched by him until the fire had sunk to red embers. I dared not leave him, yet nature, exhausted by two years of labour and by this last unnatural night, at length exacted her due. My head declined upon my breast in the chair where I sat, and I slept, if that troubled stupor may be called sleep, while the being whom I feared sat waking beside me.

I was roused by a weight descending gently over my knees and breast. By the grey dawn that struggled through the shutters I saw the coverlet from my bed drawn up towards my chin, and the creature crouched beside my chair, withdrawing his hand as though he feared he had offended. He had risen in the darkness and, remembering what I had done for him, had endeavoured, clumsily and silently, to render the same office to me. I gazed upon him, and tears—tears such as I had not shed since childhood—rushed into my eyes. He was hideous; no change of feeling could alter that dreadful truth. But the hand which I had imagined raised to destroy me had sought only to shelter me from the cold.

The church clock struck six. The rain had ceased, though the streets below were black with wet, and a comfortless light revealed how much necessity had already grown around my act. My new charge required food, clothing larger than any I possessed, and concealment from every eye in the house. I pointed to the floor, pressed my palm downwards in token that he should remain, and closed the workshop door between us. The sound of the key drew from him a low, anxious murmur, but he did not follow me.

I went out to purchase bread, milk, and such coarse garments as might be obtained without exciting inquiry, and my path led me past the inn where the diligences arrive. A coach was approaching from the far end of the street; as it drew near, I perceived that it was the Swiss diligence, and no sooner had it halted than the door was opened and Henry Clerval sprang into the yard and caught me in his arms. "My dear Frankenstein," he exclaimed, "how glad I am to see you! How fortunate that you should be here at the very moment of my alighting!"

For one blessed instant I forgot everything except that he was there. My father, Elizabeth, and the scenes of home returned upon my thoughts with him, and I felt something of the calm joy which for many months had been a stranger to my bosom. He told me, laughing, how hardly his father had been persuaded that book-keeping did not comprehend all useful knowledge, and how affection had at length prevailed where argument failed. But when he looked more closely into my face his gaiety vanished.

"You are ill," said he. "So thin and pale! You look as if you had watched for several nights."

"I have been deeply engaged in one occupation," I replied, "but it is finished. Tell me of my father—of Elizabeth—of my brothers."

"All are well, and all complain, with justice, of your silence. But first you shall breakfast with me, and afterwards show me this college room of which I have heard so much."

I urged the disorder of my apartment, the dampness of the morning, the superior comfort of the inn—every pretext that terror could invent—but Clerval only took my arm the more firmly. "If your room is disordered," said he, "we will disorder it together. Lead the way."

Never did I ascend those stairs with steps so reluctant. I knew that he whom I had left behind the locked door would know my tread; I knew also that I could not send my friend away without awakening suspicion more dangerous than discovery. When I turned the key, the inner door was already opening. The creature stood within, wrapped still in my cloak, and at sight of a stranger uttered a hoarse cry and raised both hands before his face.

Clerval recoiled, snatched up his walking-staff, and would have struck had I not thrown myself between them, my back against that trembling breast, my arms extended to cover as much of him as my lesser frame could shelter. "Do not strike him!" I cried. "Henry, for God's sake, do not strike him. He has harmed no one."

"Victor, what is this?" gasped Clerval, his face white as death. "What fiend have you concealed here?"

The creature, as if divining that I stood in peril for his sake, laid one vast hand upon my shoulder to steady me, for I swayed where I stood; and the gentleness of that support accomplished what my words could not. Clerval lowered his staff by degrees, though he did not loose it. "He has harmed no one," I repeated. "I would have fled from him last night; may Heaven forgive me, for I had already done him a greater wrong. Henry, I have bestowed life upon lifeless matter. Ask me not by what means—I will never impart that secret to living soul—but what stands before you lives because I willed it, and I cannot now unwill my responsibility."

A long silence followed, broken only by the creature's hard breathing. Clerval looked from me to him, and in his countenance horror struggled with that faithful affection which had brought him across Europe to my side. "You are half dead with hunger and watching," he said at last, more quietly. "Sit down. I will not betray you—not today. But Victor, what is to become of him? You cannot keep a giant hidden in a college room as one hides a forbidden book."

"I must teach him," I said; and as I spoke, the determination grew within me even while I trembled at its burden. "I gave him senses and no knowledge, strength and no guide. Until he can understand men, he must not go among them; and until he can speak for himself, I must not speak of him to those who would destroy him from fear."

Clerval's eyes returned to the bowed figure behind me. "Then," said he, "we must begin by keeping his creator alive." And though he still shrank from the creature's nearness, he set bread before me with his own hands.

***

Three days have passed since that morning, days divided between concealment and instruction such as no schoolmaster ever undertook. Clerval has told the porter that I am suffering from a nervous complaint and must not be disturbed; beneath his cloak he brings our provisions, and his visits, which any friend might make to an invalid, excite no remark. The creature now knows the names of bread, of water, of fire; he knows *Victor*, and turns his head when Clerval is named, though the sound he forms in answer is still rough as a stone unshaped. Last night Clerval brought, hidden among his own books, a little elementary volume with woodcuts, such as children use at Geneva.

This evening I cleared the table of every instrument that could recall the work of November, and placed that book upon it between us. Clerval stood within the doorway, watching in silence, while the creature bent his great head over the page. My fingers closed round one of his and carried it slowly along the first black character, from curve to stem, until it rested beneath the letter; and as he looked from the sign to my face, and essayed its sound, his finger pressed the paper with a care that seemed afraid to tear what it could so easily have crushed.
