chapter.chapter:
Holmes was upon the point of answering when his head turned sharply towards the house. The kitchen light, which had burned steadily behind its latticed panes, was suddenly obscured, as though someone had passed between the lamp and the window. An instant afterwards a black oblong showed where a side door had opened in the shadow of the wall, and closed again without a sound.

“Down!” whispered Holmes.

We were already crouching among the rocks, but Lestrade, who had half risen, sank noiselessly beside us. Across the dark garden a figure moved swiftly, keeping close to the orchard wall. It was a woman, tall and slim, with a dark cloak thrown over an evening dress and her hair uncovered to the wind. In one hand she carried a stable lantern, so closely shuttered that only a thin blade of light escaped; under the other arm was a bundle of some kind, from which came a faint wooden clicking as she walked.

I knew her before the moonlight caught her face. It was Miss Stapleton.

She did not turn towards Baskerville Hall, nor yet towards the gate by which Sir Henry would presently depart. At the end of the orchard she slipped through a gap in the hedge and took a narrow lane which ran, dark between banks of gorse, in the opposite direction.

“The mire,” said Holmes, under his breath. “Watson, Lestrade, come—and not a stone displaced.”

We followed at a distance, Holmes first, feeling his way over the rough ground with the certainty of a man who had learned the moor by night as well as by day. The woman walked quickly, but without hesitation, as one who knew every turn of the track. Before us the great white bank of fog lay over the Grimpen Mire, and above it the moon rode in a clear sky, silvering the upper vapour and leaving the earth beneath in a cold and uncertain twilight.

The lane ended at a low stone, half sunk in the peat. Beyond it a narrow tongue of firmer ground ran out into the bog, losing itself in fog. Here and there along its course stood slender sticks, their upper ends peeled white, so that even in the gloom they showed as a line of pale points winding away from tuft to tuft.

Miss Stapleton set down her lantern, gathered her skirts closely about her, and stepped out upon the tongue. She went forward cautiously, trying each foothold with a stick before she trusted her weight to it. At the third of the white-topped wands she stopped, bent, worked it loose with both hands, and flung it far out into a black pool, where it sank without a splash that we could hear. A second followed, and a third. Some she cast away; others, as she came back towards the margin, she gathered under her arm, until her bundle grew. At the last wand near the firm ground she knelt in the wet peat, with the sticks held tight beneath one arm, and wrenched until the thing came up suddenly, bringing with it a clod of black earth. For a breath she remained kneeling, her face turned towards the lighted windows of Merripit House; then she shuttered the lantern, rose, and hurried back.

Holmes touched my sleeve. “The marked path,” he murmured. “I have seen Stapleton’s servant follow those signs by daylight. Someone has closed a door behind the master of Merripit tonight.”

She came swiftly along the lane, her eyes fixed upon the house and her wet skirts brushing the gorse. She was within three paces of the broken orchard wall when Holmes stepped out upon the path before her. Lestrade and I showed ourselves at the same moment, one on either hand. She gave a stifled cry, recoiled, and the gathered sticks slipped from her grasp and rattled down upon the stones between us.

“Do not take me back!” she cried. “For God’s sake, do not take me back to that house!”

Holmes had put himself between her and the wall. “No one shall take you back against your will,” said he. “But you must tell us why you have been at the mire.”

She looked from one to the other of us, her breast rising and falling. There was mud to the knees of her dress, and one thin wrist showed a red mark, as though it had lately been gripped by a rough hand.

“You are Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” she said at last. “My husband followed you in London. He told me there was no escaping your eyes.”

“Your husband?” I exclaimed. “Miss Stapleton—”

“That is one of his lies,” she answered, and the words came with a bitterness which startled me. “I am his wife. There is no sister. My name is Beryl Stapleton.”

Holmes’s face betrayed no surprise. “That I had begun to suspect,” said he. “But why tonight, madam, and why those?” He pointed to the scattered wands at his feet.

“Because tonight he means to kill Sir Henry, and if his creature fails him that is the road by which he will fly.” She spoke rapidly now, as though fearful that her courage might leave her. “There is an island in the heart of the bog, where the old tin mine is. No stranger can reach it. We set the wands ourselves, he and I, when first we came to Merripit. By them he can find his way in darkness or in fog. I have taken away the beginning of the path. If he runs tonight, he will find the mire—and no road through it.”

“You have been locked in?” asked Holmes.

“Since before dinner. We quarrelled today, when I learned that the hound had been brought to the out-house. I saw the tin with which he makes it terrible, and—and I saw Sir Henry’s boot. He struck me, and swore that if I crossed him now he would finish with me also. For Sir Henry I was to have a headache, and to keep my room. He turned the key upon me. But there is a trellis beneath my window. It is old, yet it bore me.”

“And you meant only to cut off his retreat?”

“I meant that if he did this thing and failed, he should not creep away to laugh at you from the bog. If the night passed quietly, I could have set the wands again before he knew. But it will not pass quietly.” She caught at Holmes’s sleeve. “You must let me warn Sir Henry. You do not know the beast. It is not a dog as other dogs are. He has starved it, and beaten it, until it is mad for blood. He has Sir Henry’s scent. When Sir Henry leaves, he will loose it from the out-house, and follow to call it off when the work is done.”

Lestrade gave a low whistle. “Then we should take the house now, Mr. Holmes. We can hold Stapleton on her word.”

Holmes shook his head, his eyes still upon the lighted dining-room. “Her word, which she would be terrified into unsaying before a magistrate, and no proof that London could not laugh away. Stapleton would destroy his creature, deny his wife’s story as a woman’s hysteria, and wait for a safer night. No. Tonight he believes himself secure. For the first and last time he must act with armed men upon the path.”

“You will not have Sir Henry warned?”

“Sir Henry has chosen his walk, and would not be driven from it even by us. But he shall not walk unguarded. We shall be between him and Merripit before the hound has run fifty yards.”

She searched his face. “You have not seen it.”

“I have seen the work it did upon the moor when it hunted the convict,” said Holmes. “Describe it.”

“It is a cross—a bloodhound and a mastiff in one, and as high as a man’s knee at the shoulder. He paints its mouth and coat with a preparation which burns blue in the dark, but has no smell that will spoil its scent. Since yesterday morning it has had no food.”

“Thank you. That is clear, and it is enough. You will remain with Lestrade among those rocks. Whatever happens, you must not cry out, and you must not show yourself to your husband. Do you understand?”

“If Sir Henry is hurt—”

“Then the blame will be mine,” said Holmes, quietly. “But our pistols will speak before that hound has fairly fastened. Watson, give Mrs. Stapleton your coat. The wind off the mire is keen.”

She allowed me to wrap it round her, though her eyes never left the windows of the house.

***

The fog was now drifting steadily towards us, folding the lower slopes in white and leaving the path at intervals bare under the moon. The kitchen light went out. A little later the dining-room alone shone, a warm oblong in the darkness, and we could hear, very faintly, the murmur of voices and once Sir Henry’s hearty laugh. Mrs. Stapleton shuddered at the sound.

“He is telling him some story of the moor,” she whispered. “He can laugh while he does it. Oh, I know him so well.”

Holmes had drawn us slowly back along the track, as the vapour advanced, until we reached a rise where a shoulder of granite stood above the road and the path below lay clear for a little space before it dipped again into the fog. There he disposed us: Lestrade and Mrs. Stapleton in the shadow of the rock, himself and me lower down, where the track narrowed between banks of heather.

The front door of Merripit opened. Two figures stood for a moment in the yellow light. I heard Sir Henry refuse, still laughing, some offer of a lantern or a trap, and Stapleton’s answering protest, smooth and friendly. They shook hands. Sir Henry came down the drive alone, his cigar glowing, his stick upon his arm, walking with the brisk step of a man who is glad to be in the open air after a long dinner. Stapleton watched him to the gate, then turned, not into the house, but round the corner towards the out-buildings.

Mrs. Stapleton’s hand closed upon my arm with the strength of terror. Holmes raised a finger. No sound came but the slow drift of the fog and the retreating steps of our friend.

Sir Henry passed so close that I might have touched him. His face was pale in the moonlight, and he glanced back once, as a man may who feels an uneasiness he cannot name; then the fog took him, and the click of his boots sounded fainter upon the path towards Baskerville Hall.

Holmes leaned forward, his revolver cocked. “Now,” he breathed.

At first there was nothing. Then, from the white wall behind us, came a thin, crisp pattering, light and rapid, as of feet which scarcely touched the ground. It drew nearer. A shape broke from the vapour—low, black, enormous, with two burning points for eyes and a muzzle outlined in pale, flickering fire. It passed our hiding-place at a bound, its nose down, silent now save for the rush of its breathing.

Sir Henry had heard it. I saw him through a rift turn and throw up his hands. The creature gathered itself and leapt. Holmes and I fired together, and the report of our pistols crashed out across the moor. The hound was checked in mid-air, screamed—if a brute can be said to scream—and fell, rolled, and was up again, snapping at the air. It hurled Sir Henry to the ground and was at his throat when Holmes, running in, emptied his revolver into its side at arm’s length. With a last convulsive bound it fell across the path, its great limbs pawing, its flaming jaws close to my friend’s face; then it stiffened and lay still.

I was beside Sir Henry in an instant. His collar was torn, but the skin beneath was unbroken; he had swooned from the shock rather than from any wound. Mrs. Stapleton had broken from Lestrade and was on her knees beside him, calling his name with a wild mingling of terror and relief. He opened his eyes and stared first at her, then at the monstrous thing which lay smoking faintly in the moonlight.

“My God!” he whispered. “What was it?”

“Dead, Sir Henry,” said Holmes. “And I must ask your forgiveness for the use I have made of you tonight. I looked for a dog; I did not look for that.”

Sir Henry tried to rise, but his knees gave beneath him and he sank back upon the heather, shivering in every limb. Lestrade produced his flask, and after a mouthful of brandy some colour came back into his cheeks.

It was at that moment that a footstep crunched upon the path behind us.

Out of the fog, twenty yards away, a man had come to a halt. Even in that dim light I knew the slight, alert figure, the turned-up coat collar, the short leash dangling from one hand. He stood staring at the black mass upon the path and at the group about it. Holmes sprang to his feet.

“Stapleton!” he cried.

The man wheeled and ran.

“Watson, with me! Lestrade, stay with Sir Henry!” shouted Holmes, and we were off down the track, the fog closing and opening before us in fantastic wreaths. Stapleton knew every inch of the ground. More than once I saw his figure dart across a moonlit space only to vanish as I raised my pistol, for Holmes had cried to me not to fire blindly in the mist. He did not make for the door of Merripit House. As we came abreast of the orchard he swerved sharply to the left, through the gap in the hedge, and along the lane by which his wife had gone.

“The mine!” gasped Holmes. “He makes for the mire!”

We reached the low stone at the lane’s end in time to hear him splashing among the tufts ahead. The fog had for an instant thinned, and by the fitful moon I saw him stoop, grope with his hands where the first white wand should have stood, and rise with a look over his shoulder. Holmes’s voice rang out, hard and clear:

“Stand! It is useless, Stapleton!”

He answered with a cry which was half rage and half fear, and plunged forward. I saw him leap from one dark tuft to another, counting, perhaps, upon a memory which the fog and his own haste betrayed. His foot came down upon bright green moss where no firm peat lay. There was a soft, sucking sound, a frantic struggle, and then he was still—sunk to the waist in the quivering bog, his arms spread wide, his fingers clawing into a tuft of rushes which bent but did not break under his weight.

Holmes dropped flat upon the firm edge and thrust his cane towards him, while I held his ankles; but a dozen feet of black water and shaking slime lay between the cane’s end and those clutching hands.

“Do not struggle!” Holmes shouted. “Every movement takes you deeper. Lie forward upon the tuft.”

Stapleton’s face, white and mud-stained, turned towards us. “Holmes!” he cried. “For God’s sake, a rope! I am going down!”

“You are held fast enough if you keep still. We will have you out at daylight.”

“Daylight! I shall be dead!”

A woman’s cry answered him from behind us. Mrs. Stapleton, with Lestrade at her heels, came running along the lane, my coat trailing from her shoulders. She would have gone straight out upon the tongue had not Holmes risen and caught her.

“No,” said he. “That would be two lives for one.”

She stood trembling, staring at the dark shape in the bog. “Lean upon the rushes!” she called. “Put your breast upon them—so! When we set the wands, there was a root beneath. It will bear you if you do not fight it.”

“Beryl!” Stapleton’s voice was suddenly lower, and with an entreaty in it which I had never heard from him. “Beryl, you would not leave me here.”

Her hands were pressed to her face. “I took away the wands,” she said, in a tone so low that only those nearest heard her. “God forgive me, I did not know that it would be like this.”

***

We took Sir Henry into Merripit House and laid him upon the sofa in the dining-room, where the remains of his dinner with his would-be murderer still stood upon the table. The old manservant, Anthony, had gone—cowl, boots, and a full valise missing from his room, and the back door ajar. A frightened cook warmed blankets and made coffee, while Holmes, Lestrade, and I went through the out-house by lantern light. There was a heavy chain fastened to a ring in the wall, a dish of clean water, gnawed bones in a corner, and upon a shelf a saucer containing a soft paste which glimmered faintly as Holmes stirred it with a straw. Beside it lay a well-worn brown boot, the leather marked by great teeth. Holmes wrapped it in a duster without a word.

In Mrs. Stapleton’s bedroom above, the key was still in the outside of the lock. The window stood open to the night, and a green leaf from the trellis lay upon the carpet. Stapleton’s own room held a carpet-bag packed with money, a railway timetable, and papers folded ready to his hand; but of his wife there was only the silence of the house and, from far across the moor, at long intervals, the voice of the man in the bog calling upon names which no one answered.

Watson the doctor warred with Watson the companion of Holmes that night. Twice I would have risked the path in the darkness, and twice Holmes drew me back from peat which shook under a cautious toe like jelly in a bowl. “Our prisoner is in a vice, Watson,” he said. “It will neither tighten nor loose while he is quiet. A dead rescuer will not soften it.” So we kept watch in turns at the margin, with a lantern hooded upon the stone, and spoke to the wretched man when his courage failed, bidding him husband what strength remained. Towards three o’clock his calls ceased, and for an hour we feared the worst; then, as the cold deepened, came a faint moan which told us that he still lived.

With the first grey of morning the fog began to lift in ragged sheets. Mrs. Stapleton, who had refused to leave the lane’s end, came forward, her dress black with peat, her eyes hollow from watching. “I can find the way,” she said. “The wands are gone, but I know the places. There is the black pool first; keep it upon your left until you reach the cotton-grass. Then bear right, where the green is brightest and most treacherous. My husband will be beyond the second turning.”

Holmes took a coil of clothes-line from the stable and a long pole, while Lestrade and I unhinged a broad door from an empty stall to serve as a plank. With the rope fast about his waist, Holmes went first, sounding every step, laying the door where the ground seemed least firm, and working slowly out until he could reach the prisoner. Stapleton was slumped forward upon the rush tuft, his chin near the slime, his hands locked in the roots by the stiffness of cold. Holmes dug with his fingers in the peat about his waist, passed the line beneath his arms, and made it fast; then, picking his way back over the door and the tested tufts, he regained the margin.

“Now,” he said, “all together—and steadily.”

Lestrade set his feet in the firm heather, I took the rope behind him, and Holmes, still breathing hard from his own passage, hauled with us hand over hand. For a moment nothing moved; then, with a long sucking sigh, the bog loosened its hold. The prisoner slid forward upon the plank, trailing black water and slime, and we drew him, limp and senseless, out upon the solid ground.

His pulse was feeble and his skin cold as marble, one boot gone and his clothes torn by the struggle of the night. We carried him upon the stable door to the house, where I got brandy between his teeth and hot blankets about him before the fire. He opened his eyes once, saw his wife standing in the doorway, and whispered her name; whether in appeal or in hatred I could not tell.

By the time he could sit in a chair, swathed and shivering, with Lestrade’s handcuffs bright upon his wrists, Sir Henry had come from the sofa, pale and unsteady, but with his jaw set. He would not be denied. “I have eaten his salt,” said he, “and seen what he kept for me. Let me look at him.”

Holmes placed the exhibits upon the dining-room table: the glimmering saucer, the chain, the worn boot, and the small bundle of peeled wands which Mrs. Stapleton had carried from the mire. Stapleton’s eyes travelled from one to another and rested upon his wife.

“This is some trick,” he said, hoarsely. “A dog got loose upon the moor. Am I answerable for every cur in Devon?”

“You are answerable for this one,” said Lestrade. “John Stapleton, I arrest you for the attempted murder of Sir Henry Baskerville, and for what may follow concerning Sir Charles.”

Stapleton laughed, though the sound shook with cold. “And your witness? A wife who steals out at night to pull up sticks? She is mad with jealousy.”

Mrs. Stapleton had stood silent by the table, her face as white as paper. Now she drew back her sleeve. From wrist to elbow the arm was mottled with old and recent bruises. Sir Henry gave an exclamation and half rose from his chair.

“I am no longer afraid to be called mad,” she said. “I saw him give the boot to the hound. I heard him say that before another night Sir Henry would trouble no man. And I know what he did to Sir Charles, though I learned it too late to save him. Write it down, Mr. Lestrade. I will sign it.”

Lestrade took his notebook and pencil to the table. She spoke clearly, though once or twice her voice failed when she came to her marriage and the name she had borne under Stapleton’s roof. Stapleton watched her, his mud-caked hands straining once against the steel, his eyes never leaving her face.

“Beryl,” he said at last, very softly, “think what you are doing.”

She took the pencil from Lestrade. “I have thought of nothing else all night, while you were calling to me from the bog.”

Holmes and Sir Henry stood on either side of the hearth; Stapleton, handcuffed and wrapped in his blanket, sat rigid in his chair as Lestrade turned the book towards her. Her hand trembled for an instant above the page, and then, in a firm, clear script, she wrote her name beneath the statement.

Stapleton read it upside down across the table. When Lestrade lifted him to his feet for the cart which waited outside, he went without another word, but at the door he looked back—not at Holmes, nor at Sir Henry, but at the signature which his wife had set to the page.

chapter.chapter:
The counsel was not offered once, nor in haste, nor in any spirit but that of the tenderest concern. For more than a week it returned, in one form or another, whenever Anne and Lady Russell were together: at the Lodge, in their walks, in the privacy which affection had long rendered easy between them. It was represented to her that she had been formed for a safer and more equal lot; that a connexion without fortune, without family support, and dependent upon the hazards of the sea, must expose a temper like hers to anxieties under which youth and spirits would very soon sink; that Captain Wentworth's brilliancy itself was an objection, since it made his want of prudence the more dangerous; and that her father, if he did not absolutely forbid the marriage, would give it a kind of opposition more wounding, perhaps, than a direct refusal. He would do nothing for her. She would be Anne Elliot still in name, but with none of the consideration which the name had hitherto insured.

Anne heard all this, as she had been used to hear Lady Russell on every important occasion, with gratitude, deference, and even with something of self-distrust. She did not think her friend unkind; she did not think her wholly mistaken in the evils which she feared. But by degrees, as the arguments were repeated, a conviction, quiet but unmoveable, took possession of her mind. She could discover no change in Captain Wentworth, and no fault in herself, which could justify the breaking of a promise deliberately given and joyfully accepted. To renounce him because the world called the engagement imprudent appeared to her an act not of humility, but of injustice. She had already, in obedience to Lady Russell, laid every objection before him, and had told him that if, upon cool reflection, he wished himself released, she would not reproach him for withdrawing. He had refused the release with an indignation which had only endeared him the more.

The last conversation on the subject took place in Lady Russell's own room at the Lodge. The rain had kept them within doors, and Anne, who had come with the intention of speaking what had become necessary, found her courage almost failing under the gentleness with which she was received. Lady Russell took her hand as soon as they were alone.

“My dear Anne,” said she, “I have been thinking, since yesterday, that perhaps I have not sufficiently considered how much of pain my advice must give you. Believe me, I desire your happiness more than I desire to be thought right. But happiness, my love, is not to be measured by the feelings of a few weeks. You are nineteen. You know very little, as yet, of what a life of anxious dependence would be—to watch every wind, to tremble at every list of killed and wounded, to be removed from your family, and to have no establishment which your husband's absence, or even his death, might not dissolve. Captain Wentworth believes that he shall be rich. Such belief, in a young man of spirit, is natural; but ought you to build your whole future upon it?”

Anne's colour came and went. “I have thought of all that you say,” she replied, “more, perhaps, than you suppose. I know that his profession is uncertain; I know that my father will be displeased; I know that I may have very little of what the world calls comfort. But I cannot think that I should be safer, or better, for breaking my word to him. If I had reason to doubt his affection, or his temper, or his principles, I hope I could submit to your judgment, even in this. I have none. He has altered in nothing since I accepted him, except in knowing all the disadvantages which you have taught me to place before him.”

“His sanguineness is itself a disadvantage,” said Lady Russell. “It prevents his seeing them as they are.”

“It prevents his being afraid of them,” said Anne, with a faint smile. “And if his confidence should deceive us, we must bear the consequences together. It would be harder to me to bear the consciousness that I had deceived him.”

Lady Russell was silent for a moment. “You speak as if duty were wholly on one side. Is there no duty to your father? No duty to yourself?”

“There would be no duty in marrying another man,” Anne answered; “and if I give him up now, it will not be because I think another choice wiser, but because I am afraid of poverty and of blame. Dear Lady Russell, forgive me. Nothing that you can say, though no one else has half your right to say it, can persuade me that this engagement ought to be broken.”

She had spoken at last. There was no triumph, and scarcely any firmness of voice; but there was a steadiness in the words which Lady Russell understood. She rose, walked once to the window, and came back with tears in her eyes.

“Then I have done,” said she, taking Anne's hands again. “May God bless you, my dear child, and may I be the only sufferer by my own apprehensions. I will not distress you by advice which you feel it impossible to follow. But remember, Anne, that, right or wrong, you will never want a friend in me.”

Anne could only press the hands which held hers. The victory—if victory it could be called, which left her sobbing upon the bosom of the person she most loved after the man whom that person would have separated from her—was gained.

Captain Wentworth was desired, the next morning, to attend Sir Walter at Kellynch Hall. He came from Monkford with the promptness of a man who expected no favour, but was determined to deserve one. Sir Walter received him in the library, standing with his back to the fire, and looking as if he considered the dignity of the house to be personally insulted by the necessity of the interview. After a cold inquiry into his family, his present rank, and his expectations, he desired Anne to be sent for; and when she entered, pale but composed, he addressed them both with an air of injured consequence.

“You have chosen, Miss Elliot,” said he, “to persist in a connexion which no one who has a proper regard for the family can approve. Captain Wentworth has no estate, no fortune, and no alliance that can be mentioned. I shall not, however, expose myself to the reproach of cruelty. You have my consent, such as it is; but let it be understood that I do nothing more. I shall make no settlement, provide no establishment, and contribute nothing towards an union which I consider as degrading. If you marry him, you marry his prospects.”

Frederick's eye kindled, but he restrained himself. “I ask no man's fortune with his daughter, Sir Walter,” said he. “Give me Anne, and leave the rest to my profession. I have been lucky hitherto; I shall be lucky still. Before two years are over, I hope to have it in my power to place her beyond the reach of those anxieties which you are so good as to anticipate for her.”

“You may hope, sir,” replied Sir Walter, with a bow of exquisite coldness. “Hope is a very becoming thing in a sailor. Anne, you know my determination.”

“I do, sir,” said Anne; “and I am sorry to disobey your wishes in the only way in which I am disobeying them.”

Her father turned away, as if the sight of a daughter who could prefer a naval commander to the heir of Kellynch were more than his composure could support, and they were suffered to depart without another word.

Lady Russell, having failed in her great object, now directed all her prudence to lessening the evils of the step which she deprecated. She would fain have persuaded them to wait until Captain Wentworth should be again employed; but to this neither could consent. Waiting could bring no accession of fortune to Anne; and Frederick, who might be ordered to sea at a week's notice, would not leave her in a home where her engagement was endured as a disgrace, while he was exposed to the chance of never returning to claim her. With a sigh, Lady Russell yielded even this point, and interested herself, with a mother's tenderness, in preparations which her judgment still condemned. Elizabeth professed herself too ill to attend to such vulgar distresses; Sir Walter maintained a stately silence; but at the Lodge Anne found advice, assistance, and sympathy.

They were married early in November at Kellynch church. The morning was soft and grey, and the park had that still, melancholy beauty which belongs to the close of autumn. Mr Wentworth himself, by permission of the rector, performed the service; and very few persons were present besides the servants of the two houses and one or two tenants who had desired to shew their respect. Sir Walter thought proper to appear for a few minutes, in order that no one might say his daughter had been married clandestinely, and stood near the door with the countenance of a man sacrificing himself to propriety. Elizabeth did not come. Lady Russell stood close to Anne, and, when the moment arrived, placed her hand in Frederick's with a solemnity which made her own feelings sufficiently evident. Anne trembled, but she did not falter. When she left the church as Mrs Wentworth, she turned for an instant to look back at the Hall, half seen among its trees, and felt, even in the midst of happiness, the pang of a separation which no one had blessed.

The wedding breakfast was at the Lodge. Sir Walter honoured it with a bow and departed; but Lady Russell detained them under her roof until the carriage was ready to carry them to Monkford, where Mr Wentworth had insisted upon giving up his best rooms to the young couple, and where, for a few weeks, Anne knew a happiness so complete as almost to persuade her that every fear had been groundless.

***

That season of quiet was short. A letter came from the Admiralty appointing Frederick to a sloop then fitting at Plymouth, and his delight left little room for any less sanguine reflection. “You see, Anne,” cried he, “they cannot do without me. In six months we shall be laughing at your father's library and Lady Russell's storms.” They removed together to Plymouth, where two small rooms, looking towards the water, were made cheerful by Anne's arrangement and by the constant animation of his hopes. He was on board from morning till night; she learnt the names of ropes and sails with an interest which astonished herself, and walked daily in the neighbourhood of the dockyard as if the sight of masts and rigging could bring her nearer to his occupations.

On the morning of sailing, the wind blew fresh from the sea, the flags were flying, and the stone pier was crowded with officers, sailors, and the friends of those who were departing. Frederick handed her to a sheltered place under the wall, wrapped her cloak more closely round her, and spoke, in his usual tone of confidence, of prizes, of promotion, of letters which should reach her from the first port. “Keep up your spirits, my own Anne. I shall come back with a fortune, and then Lady Russell shall confess that a sailor is not so bad a speculation after all.” The boat waited; the men had their oars in the water; he sprang in, and was rowed swiftly towards the sloop, whose sails were already loosening in the breeze. Anne stood where he had left her until his figure could no longer be distinguished upon the deck, and then went back alone to the rooms which his voice had so lately filled.

She remained at Plymouth until the first letters arrived, and afterwards, at his desire and for the sake of a more economical establishment, returned to Monkford. There her married life assumed the form which Lady Russell had predicted. She had long intervals without intelligence; she watched the newspapers with an eagerness very unlike her former indifference to public events; she knew the seasons of danger upon the coast of France, and could calculate, almost to a day, when a gale might have overtaken the vessel in which her whole world was embarked. Yet she was not unhappy. Her husband's letters, when they came, were full of life and affection; her brother-in-law treated her with the kindest consideration; and Lady Russell, though at first she saw Anne's anxiety with an “I feared it” in every look, gradually forbore to triumph in the correctness of her prognostications. Anne read, worked, played to Mr Wentworth in the evenings, and became useful among the poor of the parish; and if her cheeks were sometimes thinner than they had been at nineteen, there was an animation in her eye whenever a naval despatch was mentioned which no tranquillity at Kellynch could have supplied.

***

In the following autumn, intelligence reached Monkford that Frederick's sloop had taken several valuable prizes, and that his name had been honourably noticed. Anne was already at Plymouth, having gone thither upon the first uncertain report of his approach, when he entered the little sitting-room one evening, weather-beaten, thinner, and in excellent spirits, and caught her in his arms before she had recovered from the surprise of hearing his step upon the stairs.

“Post, Anne!” cried he, as soon as she could listen to him. “Post, and the agents talk of five thousand pounds, at the least, for my share of what we have taken. Did I not tell you how it would be? You shall have a carriage yet, and Sir Walter shall bow to me across his own table.”

“You are safe,” said Anne. “That is all that signifies.”

“It signifies a great deal more, my dear girl. It signifies that you were right to trust me, and that Lady Russell—God bless her for loving you as she does—was a little too apprehensive of your sailor.”

The news, when carried to Kellynch, produced sensations very different from those which had attended the first announcement of the engagement. Lady Russell congratulated Anne with tears of genuine pleasure, and though she never said, in so many words, that her advice had been mistaken, her manner from that hour underwent a soft and gradual change. She began to speak of Captain Wentworth's judgment as well as of his spirit, and to take an interest in his professional prospects which would once have been impossible. Sir Walter, too, discovered that post rank considerably improved a man's appearance; and Elizabeth inquired, with some curiosity, whether her sister meant to be in London during the winter.

Frederick's subsequent employments were not all equally lucrative, nor was Anne's portion in them anything but that succession of hopes and fears which belongs to a sailor's wife. She passed some months in town, some at Portsmouth, and many at Monkford and the Lodge, always ready to shorten a visit or undertake a journey when a summons from him reached her. By successive exertions, and by that happy union of skill and ardour which had early distinguished him, he rose in reputation as he rose in rank. A frigate at length rewarded him; prize followed prize; and when, in the spring of 1814, peace released him from immediate service, Captain Wentworth found himself in possession of five-and-twenty thousand pounds, with no inclination to risk, in idleness or in speculation, the fortune which Anne's confidence had helped him to win.

Charles Musgrove had, in the meantime, married Mary, and was settled at Uppercross Cottage, with two little boys and all the habits of a country life. Lady Russell still resided at the Lodge, and was now as much attached to Frederick as she had once been prejudiced against him; Sir Walter's civility increased in exact proportion to his son-in-law's consequence; and if any one at Kellynch remembered the opposition of 1806, it was remembered only to make the present harmony more striking.

***

But no prosperity in a younger branch of the family could arrest Sir Walter's own career of expense. The retrenchments so long necessary became at length unavoidable; Kellynch Hall was to be let, and Sir Walter, Elizabeth, and Mrs Clay removed to Bath. Anne grieved for the imprudence which placed Mrs Clay so constantly at her sister's elbow, but she was no longer the unnoticed inmate whose warning could be treated as impertinence; Lady Russell entertained the same fears, and there the matter rested. Admiral Croft, Frederick's brother-in-law, was at that very time desirous of settling in Somersetshire. Frederick mentioned Kellynch to him; the Admiral liked the county, Mrs Croft liked everything that promised comfort without ostentation, and the terms were soon agreed upon. It was an arrangement which contained a singular mixture of pain and pleasure for Anne. Her father's house was to pass into the occupation of her husband's family; and she, who had left it under Sir Walter's displeasure, was to return to it as the wife of the man whom he had then declared unworthy of an alliance with her.

The Crofts took possession at Michaelmas. Anne and Frederick had been spending some days at Uppercross, where Mary had received them with all her usual complaints of ill health and neglect, though neither Charles nor the Miss Musgroves could discover why she should be dissatisfied with a visit so entirely made for her gratification. From thence they drove, on the first fine afternoon after the Crofts' arrival, to Kellynch. The park looked rich and sober in its autumn colouring; the deer were feeding at a distance; the Lodge windows shone through the trees; and Anne's heart beat quick as the carriage approached the hall door.

Admiral Croft met them with his hearty, open manner, and Mrs Croft pressed Anne's hands between her own as if no welcome could be too warm. They led the way to the principal apartment, where the ponderous mirrors and family ornaments remained, but where charts, a globe, and one or two naval prints had already given notice of a new order of inhabitants. “Here we are, Frederick,” said the Admiral, looking round with great satisfaction. “Your sister has made the place ship-shape already. Anne, you must tell us where everything ought to be, for it is your ground, you know, and we are but tenants.”

“Tenants who will do the place more credit than it has known for many years,” said Frederick, glancing at his wife.

Anne could not immediately answer. She was looking at the window from which she had so often watched the approach to the Lodge, and at the seat where her mother had once sat, and feeling how completely the aspect of life may be altered while the scene remains the same. Mrs Croft, with that ready perception which had first recommended her to Anne, drew her arm within hers and carried her towards the terrace door.

“Come,” said she, “and shew me the shrubbery. The Admiral will take Frederick to admire his stables, and leave us to decide everything that is really of consequence.”

Anne laughed, and suffered herself to be led on. Frederick followed them to the threshold, and the Admiral, still talking of the excellent state of the offices, opened the door; and the four went out together into the mild autumn air, with Kellynch spreading fair and familiar before them.

chapter.chapter:
He had folded the screen back before Dorian could reach him.

Basil stood quite still, with one hand still upon the screen, looking at what his own hand had made. The morning filled the library with a clear, pitiless light. From the canvas the face looked out, unchanged in its youth and colour, save only for the mouth. Round the mouth a hardness had gathered, a faint, cruel modelling that altered the whole meaning of the head, as one false note alters a melody. The living Dorian, arrested half-way across the room, seemed suddenly to be standing in the presence of a stranger who wore his beauty and had stolen the secret of his soul.

“Basil!” he cried.

The painter did not answer at once. “Who has been here?” he said at last. “Who has touched my picture?”

“No one.”

“Do not lie to me, Dorian.” He stepped nearer to the canvas, then looked swiftly back at the young man, as though he were comparing a mask with the thing that the mask had betrayed. “I painted that mouth otherwise. I remember every curve of it. It had the softness of a nature that did not yet know cruelty. This is the mouth of a man who could watch suffering and find it interesting.”

“Perhaps your art knew more than you knew yourself, Basil. Artists are always finding meanings afterwards. It is their way of being profound.”

“No. Do not jest with me. Not about this.”

He drew a white handkerchief from his pocket, folded it once, and passed the linen lightly over the pictured lips. It came away unstained. He passed it again, pressing a little harder where the new shadow lay, and again the linen was clean. With the tips of his fingers he felt the surface near the signature, and then along the lower part of the face. The varnish was hard. There was no crack, no softness of fresh pigment, no sign that any brush had travelled there since his own.

“It has not been repainted,” he whispered. “That is the horror of it. It has not been repainted, and yet it is changed.”

“You are tired, Basil. You passed a dreadful evening, you told me so yourself. Imagination is a very unkind companion after sorrow.”

“Imagination does not alter modelling.” Basil turned upon him, and his face was ghastly. “Dorian, what does it mean?”

For a moment Dorian did not speak. Then he went past him to the door, shut it quietly, and turned the key. When he came back, Basil was still standing beside the portrait, as if he feared to be left alone with it.

“It means, my dear Basil, that you are not the only person who has a secret. You heard mine once, though you treated it as a boy’s folly. That afternoon in your studio, when the picture was finished, and Harry stood laughing by the window, I said that I would give my soul if the portrait could grow old and I could remain as I was. You heard me. You tried to stop me, I remember. But words are not always wasted merely because wise people laugh at them.”

“You cannot ask me to believe—”

“I am not asking you. The picture asks you. Look at it.”

Basil shook his head slowly. “It is impossible. It is a madness that has come upon us both because of this terrible death.”

“I found it on the morning after I had seen Sibyl for the last time,” said Dorian. “She had played badly because she had learned what love was, and I told her that she had killed my love. I used phrases to her, Basil—beautiful, heartless phrases. Harry would have admired them. I came home and slept as soundly as a child. When I went to the portrait next day, the cruelty of what I had said was written there. It was written before I knew that she was dead. It was there before Harry brought me the news. Do you understand now? The thing has taken the print of my life. It bears what I choose not to bear.”

“Oh, Dorian, Dorian, do not say such things!” cried Hallward. “If there is any truth in this awful mystery—if that canvas has become the visible record of your soul—then it is not a thing to be hidden behind a screen and talked of as if it were a curiosity. There is still time. There must be still time. You are young. You were good once. You can be good again.”

“You are very dramatic, Basil. It is a quality I have always envied in you. You make remorse sound like a fine part in a play.”

“Do not talk in Harry’s voice. It does not suit you, whatever you may think. If you have injured that poor girl, pray God to forgive you. Go to her mother. Tell her everything that a man may tell without adding another wound. Refuse nothing that sorrow asks of you. It is not phrases that will save you now. It is humiliation, perhaps. It is pain.”

He caught Dorian by the hand and sank upon his knees before the portrait, drawing the young man down with him by the force of his distress. Dorian knelt, more in astonishment than in obedience, his eyes fixed not upon the floor but upon the pictured mouth.

“Let us pray,” said Basil, in a broken voice. “We are neither of us fit to choose fine words. Lord, if ignorance has led us into sin, teach us sorrow. If this boy has done a wrong that cannot be undone, let remorse enter into his heart before the heart is closed. Do not let beauty become eternal corruption. Give him back his tears.”

There was silence. Somewhere below, a servant moved a chair, and the small common sound seemed to widen the unreality of the room.

“Amen,” said Dorian softly.

Basil lifted his head. Dorian was smiling, with that exquisite, untroubled smile which the portrait no longer possessed. His hand lay cold and passive in the painter’s clasp.

“You feel nothing,” murmured Basil.

“I feel that the room is very warm, and that you will hurt your knees if you remain on the carpet. Prayers are charming things, Basil, but they belong to an age when people believed that heaven kept a ledger. I have tried sorrow. It lasted one afternoon, and bored me.”

Hallward rose slowly to his feet. A kind of terror had come into his eyes, not now for the picture only, but for the living youth who stood before him, so fair, so calm, and so untouched.

“Then the evil must be ended here,” he said. “It is my work. Whatever has entered into it, entered through me. I will destroy it before it destroys you.”

He crossed to the breakfast-table, snatched up one of the silver knives that lay beside an untouched plate, and turned back towards the canvas with the blade raised. Dorian was upon him in an instant and had seized him by the wrist. The knife shook between them, catching a thin line of sunlight.

“Basil, are you mad?”

“Let me go!”

“Once before, in your studio, you took up a knife against that picture, and I begged you to spare it. You were merciful then because I cried like a boy. Be merciful now because I am afraid. Do you know what you would cut? Do you know what bond there may be between that painted thing and the life that stands before you? It has altered when I have altered. It has taken shame upon itself so that I need not wear it. If your knife went through its heart, Basil, whose heart would answer?”

The painter’s arm relaxed. The knife fell upon the carpet with a dull sound, and he covered his face. “What have I done?” he groaned. “What have I done?”

“You have painted a beautiful picture, Basil. That is your crime, if you insist upon having one.”

“No. When I worked at it, I put more into it than colour and form. I have never told you. I could not tell you. I worshipped you, Dorian, with a worship that asked nothing and hid itself from fear of being understood. I thought that the picture had betrayed me, that any one who looked at it would see the idolatry of an artist for the one face that had made art new to him. That is why I shrank from exhibiting it. God forgive me, perhaps it has betrayed us both. Perhaps my sin found a shape in your beauty, and your wish gave it leave to live.”

Dorian’s expression softened into something almost like tenderness. “Then it is yours as well as mine, Basil. You cannot go out of this room and leave me alone with your sin.”

“What would you have me do?”

“Help me to hide it where neither servants nor friends can come upon it. Not for ever. Only until we know what this thing is, and whether it can be undone. Give me your word that no living creature shall hear of it from you—not Harry, not any priest, not any curious philosopher of souls. Tomorrow, if you wish, you shall come again, and we will talk like reasonable men. But to-day you must help me.”

“I am to be silent while you—”

“While I live, Basil. That is what it amounts to. You have always wished to share my life.”

The bitterness of the words seemed to wound Hallward even while it bound him. He looked once more at the portrait. “I will be silent for to-day,” he said at last. “I will help you to hide it. After that, God must show me what to do. I cannot promise to abandon you to this.”

“I shall never let you abandon me now,” answered Dorian.

From a drawer in the writing-table he took a key that was seldom used. He unlocked the library door, listened for a moment in the passage, and, finding it empty, drew from the end of the sofa a coverlet of purple brocade worked with gold pomegranates. Together they lifted the portrait from its place. The brocade fell over the face as Dorian threw it across the frame, shutting out the cruel mouth and the bright, accusing eyes.

It was heavier than either of them had expected. Basil took the lower part against his shoulder, and Dorian went backwards up the wide staircase, guiding the gilt edge with careful hands. Half-way up, a door closed somewhere in the lower part of the house, and they paused, not daring to breathe, with their strange burden between them. No one came. The sunlight lay in broad bands upon the carpet, and from a distant room came the muffled striking of a clock.

At the top of the house Dorian fitted the key into a door at the end of a narrow passage. The room within had the smell of shut summers and forgotten lessons. Dust lay upon the shutters and upon a small desk scored with initials. A faded map hung crookedly upon one wall, and in a corner stood a heap of books tied with string. Through a crack in the blind a blade of daylight fell across the floor. They carried the portrait in and lowered it against the wall, Basil’s hands trembling under the weight, Dorian’s face white but resolute above the brocade.

For a while neither spoke. Basil stared at the covered shape as though he could still see through the purple and gold to the face beneath.

“You will let me come to-morrow?” he said.

“I have promised you the truth, Basil. I have not promised you the key.”

Dorian went out first. In the passage he locked the door and put the key into his pocket. Then he turned, and the sunlight touched his hair and his clear, unworn mouth. He smiled as innocently as a boy who has been forgiven some trifling fault.

Basil followed him down the bright staircase, and at the first landing looked back once at the shut door, far away in the shadow at the end of the passage.
