Poole’s axe had already risen above his shoulder when Mr. Utterson caught him by the sleeve and bore the weapon down again. The butler turned upon him a face so white and haggard that, for an instant, the lawyer feared the man would strike at him in his terror; but the old habit of service prevailed, and the axe sank harmless till its head rested against the stair.

“Stay,” whispered Utterson. “Not yet.”

“Sir,” returned Poole, in the same strangled tone, “you heard it. That was never my master.”

“I heard it,” said the lawyer; “and I know the voice again. I have spoken with that man before. If we break the door upon him now, we shall have blood, or worse than blood, upon our hands before the minute is out. He has asked for mercy; let us see what mercy may purchase.”

Poole stared at him as upon one who had taken leave of his reason. “Mercy for *him*?” he said.

“For the sake of what may yet be learned,” replied Utterson. “A dead man can tell us nothing of Henry Jekyll.”

He turned his face upward to the closed door, and though his heart beat so thickly that he felt it in his throat, he spoke with a slow and studied clearness, as one who addresses a jury upon a point of life and death.

“Mr. Hyde,” he said, “you know me. I am Gabriel Utterson. You have asked for mercy in God’s name, and I am come to offer what mercy a man in your extremity may still receive at my hands. No blow shall be struck while I stand between you and harm. Open the door, come forth of your own accord, and tell me where I shall find Dr. Jekyll.”

There was a silence above, so profound that Utterson could hear the candle gutter at his feet and Poole breathing hard beside him. Then there came a short, broken laugh from behind the panels, so unlike mirth that the lawyer’s flesh prickled upon his bones.

“Utterson the lawyer,” said the voice, “pleading at a keyhole! This is a new road to the gallows. You have brought Poole with an axe, and Bradshaw, I’ll swear, skulking with a stick beside the laboratory door, and you talk to me of mercy. Your mercy would have a rope at the end of it.”

“If you remain where you are,” returned Utterson, “there will be no need of mine. How long do you think this house can be kept from the police? The servants are gathered like sheep in the hall; not one of them but believes a murder done under this roof. To-night or to-morrow some tongue will wag beyond these walls, and then the law will come with other instruments than an axe, and with less patience than I show you now. You are caged, Mr. Hyde. Your choice is between a mob of frightened servants and a friend of Henry Jekyll’s, who will see you neither beaten nor betrayed into hands that would tear you limb from limb.”

“A friend of Henry Jekyll’s!” cried the voice, with a sudden access of rage. “Ay, there it is. It is always Jekyll, Jekyll, Jekyll. What friend has Hyde in the wide world but himself?”

“Then let Hyde help himself by the only door that stands open,” said Utterson. “Tell me what has become of Jekyll. If he lives, conduct me to him, and I will forget, for that hour, every other relation in which you and I may stand. If he is injured, let him be tended. If”—he paused, for the word was bitter in his mouth—“if he is dead, then for God’s sake let his body be found by friendly hands, and not dragged forth at the heels of a constable.”

A sound followed, as of a hand beaten sharply against wood. “Jekyll is where Utterson will never lay a finger on him,” said Hyde. “Jekyll is safe from you, and from Poole, and from all the prying tribe of you. Do you think I do not know why you coax me with your lawyer’s honey? It is that I may open and be knocked on the head for the murder of Carew, and Jekyll’s friend may wash his hands of the matter with a very good conscience.”

“I give you my word,” said Utterson, “and it is a word that has never yet been broken to living man, that if you open peaceably you shall not be struck. You shall be heard. If there is a defence, you shall have counsel to make it; if there is madness, physicians to declare it.”

“And if there is neither?” asked the voice, grown of a sudden very quiet.

“Then you must abide what follows,” said the lawyer. “But even then it shall follow in the order of the law, and not by an axe in the dark.”

Poole laid a hand upon his arm. “Mr. Utterson,” he whispered, “for the love of Heaven, do not trust yourself to that creature’s promises. I saw it among the crates, sir, doubled like a monkey; and if it was not a man, it was something that should not walk God’s earth in the shape of one.”

“I am not trusting to his promises,” returned Utterson, without lowering his voice. “I am appealing to his necessities.” And again he addressed the door. “You have heard Poole. You know the temper of the house. I alone stand between you and it. Will you come down, or must we come up?”

There came a pacing overhead, quick and light, the same singular footfall which had gone up and down, up and down, through so many nights of watching; it halted close behind the panels. “If I open,” said Hyde, “it shall be upon my own terms, and Utterson shall swear to them.”

“Name them,” said the lawyer.

“Poole is to go down. The axe is to go down with him. I will not parley with a butcher at the stair-foot. Bradshaw is to be called off from the laboratory door”—Utterson started, for the man spoke as though he saw through stone walls—“ay, I heard your dispositions, lawyer; your voice carries finely through a theatre. And you yourself are to come up alone, without that poker in your hand.”

“Bradshaw stays where he is,” said Utterson firmly. “That door is your only outlet, and it shall be guarded. I will not aid you to escape into the night; I offer you safety, not liberty. But Poole shall withdraw, and his weapon with him, and I will lay aside mine.”

There was another pause. “And if I choose to keep my door shut after all?”

“Then,” said Utterson, “I have kept faith with God and with my own conscience in the offer, and Poole may do his office. It shall be upon your head.”

Something grated softly within, whether of a chair displaced or a hand upon the bolt Utterson could not tell. “Alone, then,” said Hyde at last. “Send the man down, and come up alone.”

The lawyer turned to Poole. The butler’s eyes were fastened upon him with an expression of such entreaty and horror commingled as he had never seen in a human countenance. “Sir,” he said, “you are about to put your life in the power of—”

“I am about to do my duty by my friend,” interrupted Utterson, “if any trace of my friend remains in that room. Lay down your axe, Poole.”

For a moment the man did not obey. Then, with a gesture in which twenty years of fidelity seemed to struggle against his judgment, he stooped stiffly, placed the weapon upon the bottom step, and drew back step by step into the gloom of the theatre, where the candle, set upon a crate, made a small island of yellow light among the lumber and the bottles. The lawyer himself stooped, laid the poker beside the axe, and straightened his coat with a hand that he was angered to find unsteady.

“Now, Mr. Hyde,” he said, “I am coming up.”

The stair seemed longer than he had known it; each tread creaked beneath his weight, and the red baize door at the head of it had, in the dimness, the look of a wound. He had faced angry clients, desperate suitors, men ruined and men threatening ruin, across the green cloth of his own table; he had stood, in his youth, beside a scaffold and seen a murderer die with composure. But never, until that night, had he been conscious of a fear so cold and so unreasoning as when he raised his hand and knocked, not as one demanding entrance, but as a guest who awaits permission.

“Stand back from the door,” said the voice, now so near that the panels themselves appeared to speak. “When I draw the bolt, come in quickly and shut it after you. Do you hear me, Utterson?”

“I hear you.”

Bolts were withdrawn with a deliberate slowness, as though the hand at them were weak or trembling; then the door yielded inward by an inch, and through the chink looked out a pair of eyes, sunk in a face of such a deadly pallor that the lawyer recoiled upon the landing. The next instant the opening widened, a claw-like hand descended upon his wrist, and he was drawn, rather than admitted, into the cabinet.

The door closed behind him. Hyde, with his back against it, drove the bolt home, then shrank away toward the presses as if the mere proximity of an unarmed man were a danger from which he must secure himself by distance. He was dressed, as Poole had described, in garments made for a man of far larger mould: the coat hung from his shoulders, the trousers were turned up about his ankles, and the collar gaped about a throat that looked too slender for the head it bore. Yet these incongruities, which in another presence might have moved laughter, here moved only a profound and shuddering disgust. Utterson had met the man once in a by-street and had come away with no nameable impression save that of deformity; now, in the full lamplight, with the small, snarling features working under some tempest of fear and hatred, that early antipathy returned upon him tenfold, as though nature herself protested against the thing before her.

“You see me, Utterson,” said Hyde, with a smile that was rather a baring of the teeth. “Am I not a pretty fellow to make terms with gentlemen?”

“I see a man in great extremity,” replied the lawyer, “and in great peril. Stand away from that door, and let us talk like Christians.”

“Christians!” He laughed again. “Henry Jekyll is the Christian among us. Prayers and blasphemies, Utterson; he kept them both in stock.” His glance travelled, quick as a rat’s, to a volume that lay open beside the tea things, and back to the lawyer’s face. “You are looking for him. Look, then; look your fill. There is his fire, there is his kettle singing for his tea, there is his book with his notes upon the margin. All as he left it; all waiting for the master.”

Utterson suffered his eyes to take in the chamber. It was, but for the tall glazed presses and the odour of chemicals which underlay even the smell of the fire, the most ordinary room that could be imagined: a table set forth with papers in a neat array; a drawer standing open; the kettle beginning to boil upon the hob; an easy-chair drawn cosily to the hearth with sugar already in the cup beside it. On a second table were the traces of an experiment interrupted: saucers of glass bearing measured heaps of a white salt, a paper half folded from a chemist’s packet, scales, and a graduated glass. And uppermost upon the business desk, in the doctor’s large, firm hand, lay a sealed packet addressed to *Mr. Utterson*.

The lawyer pointed to it. “What is that?”

Hyde sprang forward with a swiftness that made Utterson step back in spite of himself, and thrust the packet into a drawer, which he shut and leaned against. “Not yet,” he said. “That is for afterward. That is for when Hyde is gone and Jekyll is—where Jekyll goes.” His breathing had grown hurried; a spasm crossed his face, and he pressed both hands to his sides as a man might who endures a cramp of the vitals. “Ask your questions,” he said. “You came to draw me out; draw, then. But keep to your side of the hearth, Utterson, and do not come creeping upon me with your long lawyer’s fingers.”

“Where is Dr. Jekyll?” demanded Utterson.

“Near.”

“Alive?”

Hyde’s smile broadened. “Does that trouble you? If I say alive, you will call me liar. If I say dead, you will call me murderer. Choose the word you like best, and make a speech with it.”

“This is no time for riddling,” said the lawyer sternly. “A houseful of servants believes their master murdered. You were seen, masked and deformed, among the chemicals below; your voice has altered beyond knowledge; for a week you have cried out, by written orders, for a drug which no chemist can supply to your satisfaction. What am I to think?”

“Think that Jekyll has a malady,” said Hyde, with a mockery that rang oddly hollow, “a malady that tortures and deforms the sufferer. Those were pretty words of yours down in the kitchen, Poole tells me—no, Poole tells me nothing; I heard you through the floor, Utterson. Your voice is a penetrating instrument. A malady! Ay, you may call it so.”

“If this be a malady, come below and be tended like a man.”

“In this face?” cried Hyde. He thrust his head forward, and the lamplight showed it glistening with sweat. “Walk me through the hall, Utterson, and present me to the cook. ‘Here is your master in his affliction; kiss his hand.’ They would stone me before I reached the door; and you know it. Or walk me into the street, where every constable has Carew’s murderer by rote.”

“I do not propose to walk you anywhere as a show,” said Utterson. “I propose that you descend with me, that Poole and Bradshaw shall keep the doors, and that a carriage shall be brought to the laboratory entrance. You shall be placed, under my own eye, where physicians may examine you and where no hand shall be lifted against you till the truth be known.”

“The truth!” The word seemed to sting him. He began to pace the narrow room, from the fire to the presses and back, with that light and swinging tread which Poole had learned to dread. “You want the truth whole and ticketed, like a parcel from Maw’s. There is no carriage roomy enough for the truth of this house, Utterson.”

“Then give me so much of it as concerns Henry Jekyll.”

At the name he stopped dead. For an instant something crossed his face which was not rage and not fear, but a sort of pleading wretchedness, instantly drowned in suspicion. “Suppose I give you Jekyll himself,” he whispered. “Suppose, in ten minutes, you stood face to face with your friend, and heard his own voice, and had his own hand in yours. Would you keep your mercy then? Or is your mercy for Hyde a hook baited for Hyde only, to be drawn out of his mouth when the fish is landed?”

Utterson considered him steadily. “If Jekyll stands before me alive,” he said, “I will thank God for it, whatever company he comes in. And if you are the means of restoring him to me, even you shall not find me ungrateful.”

A low sound escaped Hyde, whether of incredulity or of a laughter that had turned to pain. “Jekyll can plead his own cause better than I,” he said. “Jekyll has a silver tongue and a clean reputation. Jekyll can weep, Utterson; it is a gift I never cultivated. Very well. You shall speak with Jekyll.”

“Produce him.”

“I am about to.”

From a press he took no key; his hand went at once, with the familiarity of long use, to the saucers upon the chemical table, turning them, comparing their contents against the light, muttering numbers to himself. One heap he rejected with a curse; a second he smelled and cast aside; over a third, smaller than the rest and lying upon a torn paper packet, he bent with a sudden and dreadful eagerness.

“This,” he said, “this may serve. Maw swore it was from a new making; the fool did not know it carried the old taint in it. A spoonful, no more.” His fingers, as he spoke, shook so violently that some of the crystals scattered and rang faintly upon the glass. “The drug has played me bitter tricks, Utterson. It loses its virtue; it demands the one impurity that made it potent, and London cannot furnish it twice over. Stand where you are.”

“What are you about to take?” asked the lawyer, advancing a step in spite of the command.

“Medicine,” snarled Hyde, “or poison; they have trod close together in this room before now.” He poured a measure of a red tincture from a phial, added the powder, and shook the vessel gently. The liquor brightened as the crystals dissolved, seethed with a small audible ebullition, and threw off a vapour that made Utterson’s eyes water; from red it passed to a dark and cloudy purple, and from purple, more slowly, to a watery green. Hyde watched these changes with a concentration so fierce that his whole small frame seemed to be gathered into his eyes. “If this fails,” he said, not looking up, “you may call Poole and his axe, and make an end in your own fashion. If it succeeds, remember your word. You shall hear Jekyll; and you shall not cry out, and you shall not call the servants in, until Jekyll himself gives you leave. Swear it.”

“I will promise to be silent while silence can save a man’s reason or his life,” said Utterson. “I will swear to nothing blind.”

“It must content me,” muttered Hyde. “It is more than my maker ever offered.”

He lifted the vessel to his lips and drained it, with a gesture in which terror and resolution were so strangely married that Utterson, who had half expected a suicide and had kept his hand ready to dash the draught away, stood arrested by the look upon the drinker’s face: it was not the face of a man destroying himself, but of one who flings himself, bound, into a flood.

Then, with a cry that rang against the glazed presses and died in a sort of animal moaning, Hyde reeled and caught at the table. The glass fell and broke unheeded. His eyes started, injected with blood; his mouth opened upon a breath that seemed to tear its way out; the hand upon the wood was knotted, the nails scraping as the fingers thickened across Utterson’s sight. *It was not pain alone*, though pain there was enough to make the sweat burst from the brow in beads; there was a horror of dissolution, as if the frame rebelled against some inward force that unmade and remade it at once. The small body shook, staggered, and—Utterson afterwards could never be persuaded that his senses had not played him false, and yet would have staked his soul upon the memory—appeared to gather bulk and stature; the face darkened as with a rush of black blood, the features ran and altered as wax alters near a flame, the stooping shoulders rose, the swamping garments filled and settled upon ampler limbs.

Utterson sprang back till the cheval-glass received him, and threw up both arms before his eyes, as a man shields himself from a lightning flash that has fallen too near. A groan, deeper now and in a changed register, broke from the figure by the table; there was a sound of tearing cloth at one seam, of a chair overturned, of breaths drawn in long, sobbing gasps. Then silence, save for the kettle singing upon the fire and the lawyer’s own heart hammering in his ears.

When he lowered his hands, Henry Jekyll stood before him.

He stood, swaying slightly, in the clothes which a moment before had trailed grotesquely upon a dwarf; now they hung upon his tall and well-knit person in folds disordered by that unspeakable passage, one sleeve rent at the shoulder, the collar twisted awry. His face was pale as a corpse’s, his hair dishevelled, his hands, which had been Hyde’s hands, and yet were now long and shapely and unmistakably the hands Utterson had clasped at a hundred dinner-tables, were pressed against his breast as though to still its labour. He looked upon the lawyer, and the expression that dawned in his eyes was that of a man who wakes in a strange place after a nightmare and finds a friend beside the bed.

“Utterson,” he said, in his own voice, hoarse but unmistakable, “God forgive me; you have seen.”

The lawyer could not answer. He was a man little given to superstition; his profession had inured him to monstrous deeds, but not to monstrous natures. A moment since, Edward Hyde had stood snarling across the hearth; now Henry Jekyll, his friend of twenty years, breathed and wept in the same air, and the discarded likeness of the smaller man seemed still to linger, like a shadow, in the set of the mouth and a certain shrinking of the shoulders. It was not belief that failed Utterson; it was the ground of the world under his feet.

Jekyll took one step toward him and sank, rather than sat, into the easy-chair by the fire. He covered his face. “Do not come near me,” he said. “I am not fit—God knows what I am fit for. Only do not call Poole yet. Not yet.”

From below there rose a clamour: Poole’s voice, uplifted in a shout, and the sound of feet upon the stair. The cry that had accompanied the change had carried, as every sound of that cabinet was wont to carry, through theatre and yard. Poole beat upon the outer side of the door—not with the axe, Utterson noted with a mind that fastened upon trifles as drowning men upon straws, but with open hands. “Mr. Utterson! Mr. Utterson, sir! Open, in Heaven’s name!”

“Answer him,” whispered Jekyll, without uncovering his face. “Tell him you live. If he forces his way and finds me thus, with the drug still upon me, I shall go mad in earnest.”

“I live, Poole!” cried the lawyer, and his own voice sounded strange in his ears. “Stand off from the door. You shall have your master presently.”

There was a murmur below, of relief and of questioning, and the feet withdrew a pace or two upon the landing. Jekyll let his hands fall. His eyes were red, his cheeks wet; yet there was already returning to him that air of composed and melancholy self-command which his friends knew, and which now struck Utterson as more terrible than Hyde’s frenzy had been: for Hyde he could abhor as a stranger, but this man he loved.

“Henry,” said the lawyer at last, and the name came with difficulty, “what have I seen?”

“What Lanyon saw before you,” returned Jekyll, “and would not write. What no man should be asked to carry in his breast alone, as I have carried it. Do not question me to-night, Gabriel; I have strength neither to confess nor to lie, and of the two, lying has been my ruin.” He leaned forward, and the firelight played upon his features, flushing and paling them by turns. “That packet in the drawer—take it. It is yours; it has been yours for more days than I can bear to count. If I disappear again, read what Lanyon left for you, and afterwards what I have written. If I remain—as God in His mercy grant I may remain—you shall have the tale from these lips, and judge me with your own ears.”

Utterson crossed to the desk, took out the sealed packet, and bestowed it in the breast of his coat, where it seemed to lie with a weight altogether disproportionate to paper. “And Hyde?” he said.

Jekyll shivered from head to foot. “Do not name him as if he were another tenant of the house whom I might dismiss at a quarter’s notice. He is—gone, for this hour. How long the draught will hold, I dare not promise. It was compounded from the last grains of the old salt, and the salt is spent. If I sleep, if I am crossed, if the body wearies of its master—” He broke off, and pressed his knuckles against his teeth. “You begin to perceive why a man might cry night and day for a drug, and throw back sample after sample upon his servants’ hands.”

“And Carew?” said Utterson, in a voice from which all warmth had departed.

Jekyll bowed his head until his forehead nearly touched his knees. There was a silence in which the kettle boiled over with a sudden hiss, and neither man moved to save it. “That sin is upon my soul,” he said at length, “by what hand soever the blow was struck. Do not ask me to divide what Heaven will not divide. I will hide nothing from you when the hour comes; but if you love the man who was your friend, do not make me begin upon a scaffold in my own cabinet, with Poole listening at the baize.”

The lawyer stood a long while looking down upon him. Professional habit, private affection, horror, pity, and a duty which he owed to the dead man’s family and to the law of his country, warred within him in a tumult such as his orderly mind had never entertained. He saw, with a clearness that admitted no evasion, that by his forbearance at the stair-foot he had become, in some measure he could not yet measure, a partaker in the secret of this house; and the knowledge sat upon him like a physical burden. Yet Jekyll’s hand, stretched blindly toward him and withdrawn again in shame, decided what argument could not.

“To-night,” said Utterson slowly, “you shall have quiet, and a locked door, and my presence in this house if it can avail you. To-morrow you will tell me all. I will neither be your accomplice nor your gaoler beyond that term, Henry; but I will not deliver a sick man, raving from his drugs, to the mercy of a frightened household.”

“Sick,” repeated Jekyll, with a wan and terrible smile. “Ay; let it be sickness till the morning.” He rose unsteadily, and with hands that trembled he straightened his coat, smoothed his hair before the cheval-glass, and then recoiled from his own image as though it had threatened him. “Poole must see me,” he said. “They have thought me murdered for a week; the poor souls below have lived upon the edge of Bedlam. If I can stand, and speak, and let old Poole look upon my face, we shall at least give them back their night’s rest.”

“You are in no condition—”

“I am in the only condition in which I shall ever be fit to face them,” said Jekyll. “If I wait to be well, Utterson, I may wait till Hyde faces them in my place.”

He went himself to the door and drew the bolt, though his fingers fumbled at the iron. Poole stood upon the landing with the candle held high, the axe forgotten below, his whole aspect that of a man prepared to look upon a corpse. At sight of his master he uttered a cry so compounded of joy and terror that the sound of it ran through the building, and the candle shook in his grasp, spilling its grease upon the boards.

“Master!” he said. “O sir, master, is it yourself?”

“It is myself, Poole,” said Jekyll gently. He extended his hand, and the butler, after an instant’s hesitation that was itself a sort of agony, took it between both his own and pressed it to his forehead. Great tears rolled unheeded down the man’s face. “God be praised! God be praised! We thought—sir, we feared—there was a thing—”

“You have been frightened by my illness,” said Jekyll, “and I by my own folly in concealing its nature. It seized me with deformity, Poole; it is an affliction I would not willingly have shown to Christian eyes. Mr. Utterson has persuaded me that I have dealt cruelly by my household in hiding myself from it. The crisis, I believe, is past.”

Poole looked from Jekyll to Utterson, and in the lawyer’s set face sought and found a confirmation which he seized upon as a drowning man seizes a plank. “A malady, sir,” he said eagerly. “Ay, Mr. Utterson said as much below; a malady that tortures and deforms the sufferer. I might have known my master could be changed, and yet be my master still. But the voice, sir—the step in the night—”

“You shall not be asked to know more to-night,” said Utterson, coming forward. “Fetch Bradshaw and the boy in from the laboratory door, Poole. Your master will speak to the household himself, and afterwards you will all go to your beds. There has been no murder done in this house to-night.”

He spoke with a firmness at which he inwardly wondered; for whether his last sentence were true, in any sense that an honest man could rest upon, he would not have dared to determine. Poole, at least, asked no more. He gave the candle into Utterson’s hand, wiped his eyes with his red pocket-handkerchief, and went down into the theatre calling Bradshaw’s name in a voice from which the worst of the fear had departed.

During the interval that followed, Jekyll bathed his face at a basin in the corner and drank, thirstily and in great draughts, from a jug of cold water. The act, so common and so human, restored Utterson more than any protestation could have done; and yet, when the doctor turned from the basin with the water still shining upon his forehead, the lawyer found himself watching the hands upon the towel for a contraction, the lips for a snarl, as he would have watched a fire banked in a grate for a tongue of flame.

“You do well to watch me,” said Jekyll quietly. “Watch me always, if we are to go on together. And now let us go down. Every minute I linger, my courage leaks out of me.”

They descended side by side: Jekyll first, with one hand upon the rail, Utterson following with the candle, Poole bringing up the rear with Bradshaw and the boy clustering at his heels, much as the servants had clustered in the hall an hour before. The theatre, with its crates and bottles, lay in a darkness that seemed to breathe; the yard beyond was black and full of wind; and London hummed solemnly all around them, indifferent to the small resurrection that was taking place within those walls.

The hall was bright with firelight, as it had been when Utterson entered, and the women rose from the hearth as the party appeared in the doorway: the cook, with her apron at her eyes; the housemaid, still trembling upon the verge of hysterics; and with them the men, white and silent, each holding himself a little behind the next. At the sight of Jekyll the housemaid broke into a fresh fit of weeping, but of another sort; and the cook, crying out that God was good, made as if she would have kissed the hem of his coat, had Poole not gently restrained her.

Jekyll stood in the midst of them, and Utterson, stepping aside to the shadow of the hearth, observed him with a sort of stern compassion. The man was ghastly pale, and lines had been graven in his face during that week of seclusion which no week of ordinary suffering could have written there; but he spoke collectedly, and with the very accents to which the house had listened for twenty years.

“I owe you all an apology,” he said, “and more than an apology. I have been seized, upon a sudden, by an illness of a kind that I was ashamed—wrongfully ashamed—to exhibit even to those who serve me with affection. It disordered my appearance, my voice, and, I fear, at times my reason; and in my folly I shut myself away, and left you to imaginations worse than the truth. There has been no stranger in my cabinet. There has been no violence done to me by any living hand. What you feared, you feared from ignorance, and the ignorance was of my making. I ask your forgiveness; and I ask that what has passed within these walls may remain within them. Poole will see that you have wine, and that your fires are made up. Go to your beds. To-morrow we will endeavour to live as Christians again.”

There was a murmur, half sob, half blessing. Bradshaw, at a sign from Poole, drew off the boy toward the kitchen passage; the cook began instantly, through her tears, to give orders about hot water and gruel as though no danger could approach a house in which a meal was preparing; and the housemaid, curtseying again and again to the empty air, suffered herself to be led away. Poole remained a moment at his master’s elbow, received some low direction concerning the laboratory door, and withdrew with a countenance in which exhaustion and relief were mingled almost to the appearance of intoxication.

Jekyll and Utterson were left alone in the hall.

For a space neither spoke. The fire, which the servants in their terrors had built high, had settled into a steady glow; a log shifted and sent up a brief shower of sparks; and somewhere in the upper house a door closed softly, as the household, obedient to its master’s word, dispersed to sleep. Jekyll looked toward the sound, and a shudder passed over his frame. When he turned again to Utterson, the composure with which he had addressed his servants had fallen from him like a garment.

“You heard me,” he said. “There has been no stranger in my cabinet. Gabriel, I have lied to them in the letter, and kept the spirit only to devour myself with afterwards. There was a stranger—and there was not. God help me, there never was.”

Utterson took his hat from the peg where Poole, in the first disturbance of the evening, had hung it. The hour was late; his own house stood dark across the squares; and before him, in the breast of his coat, the sealed packet pressed like a stone against his ribs. He turned the hat once in his hands, looking at Jekyll as he did so—at the tall figure, the bowed head, the hands that clasped and unclasped themselves in the firelight. Then, deliberately, he set the hat down again upon the hall table.

“I shall not leave you to-night, Henry,” he said.

Jekyll raised his face. For one instant—so brief that the lawyer strove afterwards to persuade himself it was a trick of the shifting light—another expression looked out of it, narrow, wary, and unutterably base, and was gone. But Utterson had seen it; and he kept his hand upon the table, close beside the hat he had resolved not to take.

“I was upon my feet and had my coat half off when there came a second splash from the margin of the bathing place. One of the little people, who had been sitting in the sun at the edge of the shallows, had flung himself bodily into the stream. He went in awkwardly, with his arms beating the water, and for a moment I thought the current had got him too; then his head came up, downstream from the drifting child and a little nearer to her than I could have got by the bank. He was no swimmer, in our sense of the word. He paddled and struggled, was rolled half over, sank until the water was about his chin, and still kept doggedly turning his face towards the place where the little creature was being carried round a bend of the river.

“The drowning thing came twisting down upon him, its hair spreading in the current and its hands opening and shutting aimlessly above the surface. He met it breast to breast, thrust one skinny arm beneath its chin, and bore its head up even as his own mouth went under. I had by this time got my shoes off and was plunging in waist-deep at a point below them. The stream seized me round the knees and tried very hard to have me off my feet. A dozen yards separated us, and in those dozen yards I saw the rescuer go down twice and come up again, blue-faced and strangling, but always with that small white head held, if only for a breath, above the ripple.

“Then the pair of them swept against me. I caught the boy—for such, as I afterwards understood, he was—by the wrist, and felt at once how nearly spent he was. The current struck us sideways and drove us stumbling towards a snag of roots. His foot hit upon some stone under water, and he cried out in that small flute-like voice of his kind and almost let his burden go. I got my other arm about the child, dragged them both out of the main set of the stream, and so, half carrying and half towing them, worked towards a shelving place where the water ran brown and quiet among the reeds.

“I laid the little drowned creature upon the grass and, kneeling beside her, rubbed her limbs and pressed the water from her breast after the rough fashion one uses in such cases. The rescuer lay at her other side upon his elbow, coughing miserably, with a thin streak of blood coming from one ankle and his whole slight body shaking as if with an ague. Presently the child’s eyes opened. She did not look at me. Her hands went out at once, found his wet fingers, and held them with a convulsive tightness; and he, for all his own distress, bent over her and made a soft crooning noise in his throat. The other bathers were now about us in a ring, staring, exclaiming in their sweet inarticulate tongue, and bringing, quite uselessly, double handfuls of dripping flowers to lay upon the bank.

“It will give you an idea of the correction this incident worked in my judgment, when I tell you that I had already begun to reckon these people incapable even of the impulse to help one another. In that I was wrong. But I was not altogether wrong. This frail rescuer had had the will to save, and more courage, perhaps, than any creature of his size and strength had a right to possess; yet his courage had very nearly been the death of three of us. He could not swim. He had no more notion of economising his exertions than a child who beats at deep water with its hands. The heart, if one may call it so, had survived the enfeeblement of the race; the body and the practical intelligence had not. Left alone, he and the child would certainly have gone down together.

***

“In the afternoon I met them again as I was returning towards the great house from an exploration among the hills. I knew the drowned child by a white flower still tangled in her hair, and her companion by his limping gait and swollen ankle. They came towards me with cries of delight—not, I was presently to learn, chiefly upon my account. In a little stone arbour beside the path we sat down together, and there the girl took from her lap a great garland, evidently woven for one neck and one only, and hung it about the rescuer’s throat. She did it with an air of grave and childish solemnity, and then clapped her hands and laughed. For me she had a single blossom, which she thrust, after some hesitation, into the breast of my coat. I did my best to show that I understood the distinction and bore no malice for it.

“We fell, after our fashion, into conversation—chiefly smiles, flowers passed from hand to hand, and soft syllables repeated until I blundered into something like their sound. She kissed his bruised hands; she kissed mine also, but as one might kiss a friendly and unfamiliar animal that had been of service. I pointed to her, and after many repetitions caught a word which I render as Weena. I pointed to him, and she said another word, clearer because he repeated it himself several times, tapping his breast: Ara. My own name for myself defeated them utterly. Ara twisted his mouth round it once, produced a musical absurdity, and abandoned the attempt with a peal of laughter in which Weena joined. He was exactly like a child, and yet there was in his glance at her, whenever she winced in remembering the river, a swift protectiveness which was not childish at all.

“Towards evening his ankle had swollen so that he could not bear his weight upon it. I took him up in my arms—he weighed no more than a boy of ten—and carried him up the broad steps towards the hall, Weena trotting beside us and holding one of his hands all the way. The thing seemed to delight them both. He laid his head against my shoulder with the most entire confidence, and once, when I stumbled, his fingers tightened upon my sleeve, not in self-preservation, as it seemed to me, but as though he would keep me from falling too.

***

“It was from these two that I learnt how fear had not yet left the world. In the daylight Ara was fearless enough, after the measure of his strength; he laughed at a foolish grimace with which I tried him, and he had gone into the river with death plain before him. But as the sun sank and the shadows lengthened among the pillars, I saw a change come over him. He kept putting himself between Weena and every black doorway. He glanced over his shoulder at the deepening blue between the trees. When I made as though I would sleep upon the flagstones outside, as had been my habit, he caught my sleeve and would not be shaken off. Weena joined her entreaties to his, pulling at my other hand with all her little force, until, seeing that to persist would be to drag a lame creature out into the dark after me, I yielded and went in with them.

“Within, the Eloi—for so I learnt to call this fair-haired people of the Upper World—were gathering in multitudes for the night. They slept in droves upon the floor of the great hall, huddled together like young animals in a litter. No one, so far as I could discover, ever slept alone after dark, and to enter among them without a light was to set the whole place astir with apprehension. Weena lay down with her head upon Ara’s arm. Ara, before his eyes closed, found my sleeve again and slept with his fingers locked in the cloth, as a child might hold to its nurse in a thunderstorm. I lay awake a long while, listening to the soft breathing of that timid multitude, and wondering at a creature who could face the river at noon and tremble at his own shadow at nightfall. I was still such a blockhead that I missed the lesson of his fear.

***

“I had slept ill, dreaming that I was under the river again, with soft white fingers feeling over my face, and I rose while it was still that ghastly hour when dawn and the last of the moonlight are mingled and everything is colourless and clear-cut and yet unreal. I went out upon the flagstones to see the sunrise. The bushes were inky black, the ground a sombre grey, the sky without warmth or promise. And up the hill, as I scanned the slope, I saw figures that were not Eloi—or not Eloi as I knew them in the sunshine. Three times they showed against the paling east: white, stooping shapes, ape-like in their carriage, going swiftly among the bushes. Two went empty-handed. Between and a little behind them the third bore a dark burden across its shoulder, something that hung limp and did not struggle.

“I doubted my eyes. The dawn was still indistinct, and I had that chill, uncertain feeling of the early morning which makes a man distrust his senses. I remember that a queer notion of Grant Allen’s came into my head and amused me even then—that if every generation left its ghosts behind it, the world by this time must be overcrowded with them. But the jest would not stay. These things had weight and purpose. They crossed a space of open grass, they vanished among the ruins upon the hill, and when the full daylight came there was no vestige of them upon the slope. I associated them, in some indefinite way, with the white animal I had startled during my first passionate search for the Time Machine. But Weena was singing somewhere within the hall, and Ara, limping cheerfully into the sunshine with his ankle bound in leaves, was a pleasant substitute for phantoms. They were destined, nevertheless, to take a far deadlier possession of my mind.

***

“Later that morning the heat was very great—hotter, as I have told you, than any weather of our own time—and I sought shelter in a colossal ruin not far from the house where I slept and fed. Ara essayed to follow me, but I made him sit down in the shade with Weena, signing to him to rest his foot, and after a mournful glance he obeyed. Clambering among heaps of fallen masonry, I found a narrow gallery whose far end and side openings were blocked by masses of stone. By contrast with the brilliancy outside it seemed at first impenetrably dark. I went in groping. Suddenly I halted spellbound. A pair of eyes, luminous by reflection, was watching me out of the blackness.

“The old instinctive dread of wild beasts came upon me. I clenched my hands and stared into those glaring eyeballs and was afraid to turn. Then I remembered the apparent security of mankind in this age, and with it Ara’s terror of the dark, and overcoming my fear to some extent I advanced a step and spoke. My voice was harsh and ill controlled. I put out my hand and touched something soft. At once the eyes darted sideways and a white thing ran past me into the sunlit space behind. I turned with my heart in my mouth and saw a queer little ape-like figure, its head held down in a peculiar manner, blunder against a block of granite, stagger, and in a moment take refuge in the black shadow beneath another pile of ruin.

“My impression of it is of course imperfect; but I know it was a dull white, and had strange large greyish-red eyes, and that there was flaxen hair upon its head and down its back. I cannot say whether it ran upon all fours or only with its forearms held very low. I followed it into the second heap. There, in profound obscurity, I came upon one of those round well-like openings of which I have told you, half closed by a fallen pillar. A sudden thought struck me. I lit a match, and looking down saw a small white moving creature clinging to the side of the shaft far below, its bright eyes turned steadfastly up to mine as it retreated. It was clambering downwards, hand and foot, upon a series of metal rests that formed a kind of ladder in the wall. It made me shudder. It was so like a human spider. Then the match burnt my fingers and fell from my hand, and when I had lit another the little monster had disappeared.

“I sat upon the edge of that well for a long time before I could persuade myself that the thing I had seen was human. Gradually, however, the truth dawned upon me: that Man had not remained one species, but had differentiated into two distinct animals; that my graceful children of the Upper World were not the sole descendants of our generation, but that this bleached, obscene, nocturnal thing, which had flashed before me, was also heir to all the ages. I thought of the wells and the flickering pillars of air above the ventilating towers, and I began to suspect their true import. Beneath my feet the earth must be tunnelled enormously, and these tunnellings were the habitat of the new race. What so natural, then, as to assume that it was in this artificial underworld that such work as was necessary to the comfort of the daylight people was done?

“I dare say you will anticipate the shape of my theory, though for myself I very soon felt that it fell far short of the truth. Proceeding from the problems of our own age, it seemed clear as daylight to me that the gradual widening of the merely temporary and social difference between the Capitalist and the Labourer was the key to the whole position. Already, in our time, industry is for ever burrowing: we have our Metropolitan Railway, our underground workrooms and restaurants, our subways and cellars for the less ornamental purposes of civilisation, and they increase and multiply. Evidently this tendency had increased until Industry had lost its birthright in the sky, going deeper and deeper into ever larger underground factories, till the worker spent so much of his life therein that he was at last cut off from the natural surface of the earth. Above ground, meanwhile, the rich, pursuing pleasure and comfort and beauty, shut in the prettier country against intrusion, refined their education, intermarried less and less with the class below them, and so at last fixed the separation. Above, the Haves; below, the Have-nots, growing continually adapted to the conditions of their labour. Such of the underground folk as were miserable and rebellious would die; the survivors would become as well adapted to darkness, and as happy in their way, as the Overworld people were to light.

“The too-perfect security of the Overworlders had led them, as I could already see, to a slow movement of degeneration—to dwindling in size, strength, and intelligence—and yet, as Ara had taught me that morning by the river, not to the extinction of courage or of love. What had happened to the Undergrounders I did not yet suspect; but from what I had seen of the Morlocks—for that, by the bye, was the name by which these creatures were called—I could imagine that the modification of the human type there had been far more profound than among the Eloi. Then came troublesome doubts. Why had the Morlocks taken my Time Machine? Why, too, if the Eloi were masters, could they not restore it to me? And why were the Eloi so terribly afraid of the dark?

***

“I found Weena and Ara upon the terrace before the great house when I returned, he with his lame foot stretched before him, she weaving yet more flowers into a chain of an intolerable pinkness. I sat down beside them and tried, by signs and drawings in the dust, to question them about the underworld. I drew a circle for the mouth of a well, lines beneath for the shaft, and two round dots for eyes shining in the darkness. I pointed downwards, and then at them, and made what interrogation I could with my hands. At first they would not understand. Then Weena shivered and hid her face. Ara understood indeed. He put his arm about her with that same swift protectiveness I had seen by the river, looked once towards a bronze-rimmed well upon the slope, and spoke a word softly in his own tongue—the word I have rendered as Morlocks. His voice shook as he said it.

“I pressed him, perhaps a little harshly. He rose, limping, and pointed down into the black shadow of a doorway, and then, as though the darkness itself had answered, shrank back with his hands before his eyes. Weena burst into tears. They were the only tears, except my own, that I ever saw in that Golden Age. When I saw them I ceased abruptly to trouble them further, and was only concerned in banishing these signs of her human inheritance from her eyes. I struck a match and held it up, and presently she was smiling through her fright and clapping her hands at the little flame. Ara laughed too. But his laughter died before the match did, and his gaze went back, in spite of himself, to that well upon the hillside.

“All that evening the contrast worked in my mind like a reproach. Ara had gone into deep water for Weena although he knew—if so frail a creature can be said to know—that the water would have him. I, who prided myself upon a man’s strength and a man’s resolution, had sat upon the brink of a shaft in broad daylight telling myself that there was nothing to fear, and had been absolutely afraid to go down. My theories were very fine. I had explained the Eloi, I had explained the Morlocks, I had explained the ventilating towers and the mystery of the ghosts; and all the while the one creature who had acted upon his knowledge, such as it was, lay asleep in the hall with his fingers still, in his dreams, seeking the security of my sleeve. I determined that at noon next day, when the subterranean folk should be deepest in their slumber and the sun at its strongest above their shafts, I would go down the ruined well and see what could be seen. I had my matches. I had no other preparation to make, and—if I am honest—no other preparation that my fear would have allowed me to delay upon.

***

“I slipped away from the great house while Weena and Ara were at their fruit, but I had not climbed half the hill before I heard a light pattering behind me and, turning, saw them both. Ara came first, limping valiantly with a stick he had found, his face set in an expression of such earnest determination as would have been comic upon any other countenance. Weena followed close, grave and distressed, her hands full of flowers for which neither of us any longer had a thought. I signed to them to go back. Ara shook his head. He pointed to the river below, then to me, then, very solemnly, to his own breast, and at last down towards the ruins; and though I could not render his meaning in words, I understood well enough that he held himself bound. Weena caught at his arm as we went on.

“At the well among the stones I hesitated only long enough to strike a match and satisfy myself that the iron rests went down beyond the reach of sight. Then I swung myself over the broken rim and felt for them with my feet. Above me the daylight lay like a bright disc. Ara, in sudden terror lest I should be gone before he could follow, dragged himself to the edge and got his lame leg over the bronze, meaning to come after me though every line of him trembled at the darkness. I cried out to him to stop. Weena had him then by the arm and by the skirt of his tunic, and she held him—this child, who could not hold her own weight against a river’s current—with the strength of a terror greater than his own. I looked up at them for the space of three breaths: his white face strained towards me, hers turned wholly to him, her small hands locked and straining. Then I put my weight upon the rest below, and went down another, and another, while the dull thud—thud—thud of the engines rose out of the blackness to meet me.

chapter.chapter:
The Wizard leaned far out of the basket, with both hands stretched toward her. The ropes that held the great green bag creaked and strained, but they did not break. The soldier with the green whiskers, seeing Dorothy come running, threw his whole weight upon the anchoring rope, and two men behind him caught hold to help him, so that the basket still bumped and swayed against the ground within her reach.

Dorothy caught Toto more firmly in her arms and ran the last few steps. Oz seized her wrists and drew her upward while her feet scrambled at the wicker side, and in another moment she was safely in the basket, though she landed very suddenly upon the Wizard’s green carpet-bag. Toto stood upon her lap and barked at the crowd, as loudly as if he had done it all himself.

“Sit down, my dear, and hold him fast,” cried Oz. “We are off at last!”

Dorothy sat down with her back to the side of the basket. Beside the carpet-bag stood a covered hamper, which Oz had filled with provisions for their journey, and four small sacks of sand were tied around the outside of the basket to keep it steady. Oz, laughing like a happy boy, leaned out and waved his hat toward the Tin Woodman, who stood below with his axe in his hands.

“Now, Woodman!” he called. “Cut us free!”

The Tin Woodman lifted his axe, and with one bright stroke severed the rope. The balloon sprang upward so swiftly that Dorothy clutched at the rim and Oz sat down all at once upon his carpet-bag. A great shout arose from the people, and hundreds of green hats were thrown into the air.

Dorothy leaned over as far as she dared. Upon the Palace steps stood the Scarecrow, waving his hat with both hands, for Oz had left him to rule the City. Beside him the Tin Woodman’s polished arm flashed in the sunlight. The Lion reared upon his hind legs and sent after them a roar so loud that it reached the basket even above the cheering of the crowd.

“Good-bye!” called Dorothy. “Good-bye, dear friends!”

But whether they heard her she could not tell, for the balloon was already higher than the tallest spire of the Palace. The streets below looked like green ribbons, the houses were no larger than boxes, and the people had become tiny moving specks. Toto put his forepaws upon the rim and looked down with his ears blown back by the wind, but Dorothy held him tightly and drew him into her lap again.

Oz was still standing up and waving, although there was now no one who could see his face.

“Please sit down,” begged Dorothy. “If you fell out, I should not know how to manage the balloon.”

“That is true,” said Oz, and he sat down beside her with a sigh of content. “Not every day does a man escape from being a Wizard.”

Then, taking a little key from his waistcoat pocket, he unlocked the green spectacles that Dorothy wore, and after them the smaller pair that had been fastened upon Toto.

“You will not need these outside the City,” he said. “I brought the key with me, for I did not intend to come back.”

Dorothy blinked in the clear light. The fields below were still green and pleasant, but not so dazzlingly green as they had seemed through the spectacles, and here and there she could see white roads, blue water, and farmhouses of many colors among the trees.

“Are we going toward Kansas?” she asked.

Oz shaded his eyes and looked at the sun.

“The wind is carrying us toward the west,” he answered, “and a balloon must go where the wind takes it, for it has neither rudder nor sail. When I came to this country, the wind carried me where it pleased, and the people who saw me descend thought I was a great Wizard. Perhaps the same wind will be kind to us now. When we have crossed the desert, we may find people who can tell us the road to Kansas, or perhaps even a railroad.”

“I do not care how we go,” said Dorothy, “if only we get to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry at last.”

The basket swayed gently as they floated onward. Toto, after a time, ceased to be frightened, and curled himself upon Dorothy’s dress. Oz opened the hamper and gave Dorothy bread and cheese and a piece of cake, while Toto had a share of everything and thought the journey a very fine one indeed. There was also a bottle of water, which Oz said they must use carefully, because no one could tell how long they might be in the air.

After they had eaten, Dorothy pointed to the carpet-bag upon which she had fallen.

“What have you brought in that?” she asked.

“My clothes,” replied Oz, “and the little properties that made me a *Wizard*. Here are bottles of colored water, and strings of cups and balls, and a long false beard, and a wig, and ever so many other foolish things. If we come to a circus, I may earn my living with them again; but while we are in the balloon they will serve for company.”

Below them the road of yellow brick wound through the country like a narrow ribbon. Dorothy knew it well, for she had traveled it on foot with the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman and the Lion. Now the farms of the Winkies, with their yellow roofs and yellow fences, passed beneath them, and the fields grew yellow in the sunlight. Far away she saw a dark castle standing among the hills, and she remembered the Wicked Witch of the West, and how frightened she had been when the Winged Monkeys brought her there.

“It seems a long, long time since we walked upon that road,” she said.

“And now you are flying over it,” answered Oz. “That is the advantage of a balloon.”

Presently the Emerald City had sunk to a green spark behind them, and then it was gone altogether. Dorothy gave a sudden cry.

“Oh, what have I done?” she exclaimed. “I have left the Golden Cap in my room at the Palace! If I had brought it with me, I could have called the Winged Monkeys.”

“Never mind,” said Oz cheerfully. “There will be no need of magic in Kansas. Besides, the Monkeys might not like to carry a balloon.”

Dorothy said nothing more, but she was sorry she had left the Cap behind. In her hurry to catch Toto and reach the basket, she had never thought of it; and now the Palace was far away, and her friends with it.

The yellow country below them grew drier and more barren. The farmhouses became fewer, the trees disappeared, and at last there were no fields at all. A vast, pale desert stretched before them to the edge of the sky, with great hills and hollows of sand, and no road or river or living thing to be seen upon it.

At first Dorothy did not notice that the balloon was sinking. The ground had seemed very far below for so long that she had grown used to the sight. But presently she saw their shadow gliding over the last of the yellow fields, and it looked larger and nearer than it had before.

“Are we coming down, Oz?” she asked.

The little man stood up and put his hand upon the silk above the opening of the bag. His face grew grave.

“The air in the balloon is cooling,” he said. “The sun keeps it warm for a while, but not as the fire did. I was afraid of this, my dear.”

He took a penknife from his pocket, leaned over the side of the basket, and cut the cord of one of the sand sacks. The sand poured out in a long, glittering stream and vanished beneath them. At once the balloon ceased to sink, then rose slowly until the desert was again far below.

Dorothy, who was holding Toto fast in her lap, drew a breath of relief.

“One bag has saved us,” said Oz, “but there are only three left. We must cross as much of the desert as we can before they are gone.”

After that the balloon floated on in silence for a long time. The sand hills below looked like great yellow waves that had suddenly stood still. There were no birds in the air and no sound but the creaking of the basket and the soft flapping of the ropes. The sun beat down fiercely, and Toto panted with his little tongue out, so Dorothy moistened his mouth with water from the bottle and held her handkerchief over his head to shade him.

Twice more Oz was obliged to cut away a sack of sand. Each time the balloon rose a little, but each time it rose less willingly than before. When the last sack was gone, Oz looked over the side and shook his head.

“Now we must trust to the wind and the sun,” he said.

The sun was low when the basket began to sink again, steadily and surely. The silk bag above them, which had been round and firm, was now wrinkled, and its sides drew in as the air within it cooled. Oz tried to look cheerful, but Dorothy could see that he was troubled.

“What can we do?” she asked.

Oz opened his carpet-bag and took out the long false beard. He looked at it sorrowfully.

“These things have made me seem great for many years,” he said, “but humbug is very heavy stuff.”

He placed the hamper upon the carpet-bag and tied them together with a piece of rope. Dorothy protested that they would need the food if they came down in the desert.

“We shall need to stay in the air even more,” replied Oz. “Keep the water bottle, my dear, and hold Toto.”

The basket was swaying as it sank. Dorothy clung with one hand to the rim, while Toto was pressed close under her other arm. Oz lifted his bundle to the edge, paused for one moment, and let it fall. Bag and hamper turned over and over as they dropped, growing smaller and smaller until they were lost among the shadows of the sand.

The balloon rose slowly, as if it were tired, and for a little while they floated onward. Oz sat down beside Dorothy and wiped his forehead.

“There goes my fortune,” he said, “and our supper with it.”

“Never mind,” said Dorothy. “Aunt Em will give us plenty to eat when we get to Kansas.” But her voice trembled, for Kansas seemed farther away than ever.

The light faded quickly. As the sun touched the edge of the desert, the air in the balloon grew cold, and the green silk lost its roundness and hung in loose folds. Down and down went the basket, until Dorothy could see the separate grains of sand upon the tops of the hills.

“Sit low,” said Oz, “and hold Toto close. Brace your feet against the side of the basket.”

Dorothy crouched down with Toto in her arms. Oz knelt beside her and gripped the wicker with both hands. The basket struck the crest of a sand hill, bounded a little way into the air, and then came down again and was dragged swiftly along, plowing a deep furrow in the sand. Above them the great silk bag swayed, collapsed, and came falling down in green folds, shutting out the light.

Another bump threw Dorothy against Oz, and then the basket stopped, tipped half upon its side. For a moment neither of them spoke. Then Toto sneezed, and Dorothy laughed shakily to find that he was unhurt.

They crawled out from beneath the silk and stood upon the sand. The balloon lay spread around the basket like a great green cloak. Oz climbed to the top of the nearest hill and looked in every direction, but there was nothing to see except sand and sky. No tower of the Emerald City, no house, no tree, no river broke the empty circle of the horizon.

“I am afraid we are lost, Dorothy,” he said, coming back to her. “I have brought you into great trouble, and I am very sorry.”

“You tried to keep your promise,” answered Dorothy, “and you came with me yourself. We must wait until morning and see what we can do.”

The dusk was gathering, and the wind over the desert felt cold after the heat of the day. Dorothy looked at the fallen balloon, and then at the basket.

“We can make a tent of the silk,” she said. “It will keep the wind from us tonight.”

So together they drew the green folds over the basket, which they had set upright again, and fastened the edges down with the empty sand sacks, now filled with sand. Toto, while they worked, dug busily beside them until he had made a cool hollow, into which he curled himself with a sigh. When their shelter was finished, Dorothy gave him a few drops of water in the palm of her hand, and Oz insisted that she should drink the rest of what they could spare.

Then they sat beneath the edge of the silk and watched the stars come out, one by one, over the silent desert. Toto slept in Dorothy’s lap, and her silver shoes gleamed faintly in the starlight. Oz sat beside her, very quiet, looking toward the black horizon where neither Kansas nor the Emerald City could be seen; and the great green balloon, which was to have carried them home, stirred softly in the night wind above the basket.

chapter.chapter:
Dick had scarce risen when I knew that my hour was come. The barrel stood in the shadow between the foremast and the galley, and he had not far to go. I heard the soft rattle of his shoes upon the deck, saw his dark figure bend above me, and felt his hand go groping down among the few apples that remained at the bottom. I tried to shrink lower, till my chin was among my knees and every stave seemed to be cutting into my back, but his fingers brushed my hair, paused, and then closed hard upon the collar of my jacket.

He gave a smothered cry and dragged me half out before he knew what he was doing. My legs were dead with crouching; I reeled against the rim, and one or two apples leaped out and rolled upon the planks. Dick still held me by the collar, his mouth open and his face as white as paper in the darkness.

“Jim!” he whispered.

Silver swung round upon his crutch. For one instant the genial, chuckling cook was gone, and I saw a face so sharp and startled that it frightened me worse than Hands himself. Then, swift as thought, the look was covered over. His eyes travelled fore and aft along the deck. No officer was near us; the watch by the forecastle had his back turned, and the man at the wheel was a black shape far away under the stars.

“Why, Jim,” says Silver, very low and very pleasant, “what’s this? Come after an apple, have you, and fell asleep in the shop?”

“I never put him there, John!” Dick burst out. “I never knew—”

“Stow it,” said Silver, still smiling, but with such an edge to his voice that Dick shut his mouth at once. Silver pulled me into the lee of the fore-sail and set a great hand upon my shoulder. It rested there kindly enough to any one who might have passed, but the weight of it kept me where I stood.

Hands came close on the other side. He was looking not at Silver, but at me, and his eyes were small and bright with rage.

“He’s heard us,” says he.

“I didn’t mean—” I began, but my tongue seemed to stick to the roof of my mouth.

Hands’s hand went to the knife at his belt. “Dead men don’t bite,” he said.

The blade was half out when Silver caught him by the wrist. He forced the hand down and down, till the point was against the deck, and with his other arm across Hands’s chest he drove him back against the barrel. There they stood for a breath, face to face, Silver still wearing that horrible, fixed smile.

“You touch this lad,” he says, “and I’ll break the arm off at the socket. D’ye want Smollett to turn the ship inside out for his cabin-boy before we’ve so much as smelt the land? D’ye want us all dancing at the yard-arm for a moment’s temper? Use what head the Lord gave you, Israel.”

“I say he’s heard us,” growled Hands, but he let the knife slide home.

“And I say he may be worth more to us breathing than bleeding,” returned Silver. Then he turned to me again, and dropped upon his sound knee so that his face was level with mine. “Now, Jim, let’s have it fair and manly. How long have you been in there?”

“Since—since you began about Flint, sir.”

“What did you make of it all?”

I could not lie to those searching eyes. “I heard about gentlemen of fortune,” I said, “and—and what was to be done after the treasure was aboard.”

Dick made a little sound in his throat. Silver’s hand tightened almost imperceptibly upon my shoulder.

“Ah,” says he. “That’s bad hearing for a young lad, that is. It was rough talk, Jim, meant to keep a fool like Israel in humour and frighten Dick here out of his wits. There’s meanings in sailor talk a landsman’s boy isn’t meant to follow.”

“You said Mr. Trelawney—”

“I said a sight too much,” he interrupted, and though he smiled, there was no mirth in it. “Very well. You’ve heard what you’ve heard, and now it’s between you and me what’s to come of it. If you go running aft this minute with your mouth open, do you think these gentlemen of fortune will wait politely to be clapped in irons? Israel and his like will be through the cabin door before the captain can call for his pistols, and who’s to stand in their way? The doctor, maybe, coming up the companion with his wig in his hand. Is that what you’d purchase with your tale, Jim?”

I shook my head, too terrified to speak.

“But you lie by, and keep a still tongue till I give you the word, and old John will keep them in leash. When the blunt’s aboard, they’ll need Cap’n Smollett to work the ship home—didn’t I tell them so, not five minutes since?—and a man who wants a ship navigated doesn’t cut the navigator’s throat. There’s ways and means, Jim, ways and means of getting gentlemen ashore with whole skins while other folks are busy below. You trust to me, and I’ll trust to you. Why, you and me’s always been thick, ain’t we?”

I knew he was lying. I had heard him, not an hour before, claim the squire for his own hands; I had heard him vote for death as coolly as another man might vote for his dinner. Yet Hands was standing at my back, Dick’s face was a picture of misery, and Silver’s great paw upon my shoulder felt at once like a protection and a chain.

“Give us your hand on it, then,” says Silver, “like a lad of spirit. Same as Dick done.”

He held out his hand. At the same instant I felt the point of Hands’s knife press lightly through my jacket behind. Silver’s fingers closed round mine, warm and immensely strong.

“I promise,” I whispered.

“There’s my brave lad,” says he. “And now see here: you came for an apple, and you dropped asleep, and you heard no more than a dream of pipes and tobacco. Take this along with you and let’s see you bite it.”

He put an apple in my hand and, with a clap on the back that nearly sent me headlong, pushed me gently from the shadow of the sail.

“Dick and you’s chums now,” he added in the same easy voice. “Bear him company a bit, Dick.”

Dick came after me and laid hold of my sleeve above the elbow. He did not look at me, and his fingers trembled through the cloth. My own legs were still pricking as the life came back to them, and the apple shook in my fist.

Just then a brightness began to grow over the deck. The moon was lifting clear of the sea, silvering the tops and laying a long white road upon the water. Almost in the same moment the lookout hailed from aloft—“Land ho!”—and there was a rush of feet from forecastle and cabin alike.

Dick’s grip tightened. “Don’t you—” he began.

But the crew were pouring past us to the weather side, laughing and jostling in their excitement. A big seaman knocked Dick’s shoulder half round; the hold on my sleeve broke, and I ducked under another man’s arm and ran aft as fast as my still-tingling legs would carry me. For one wild second I thought I heard the thump of Silver’s crutch behind, but the crowd closed between us, and the next I had caught Dr. Livesey by the coat as he came hurrying up with Hunter.

“Doctor,” I gasped, keeping my voice down with all my strength, “Silver found me in the barrel. For God’s sake, get the captain and squire below. I am to go first and wait. It is worse than I can say here.”

The doctor’s face altered in a way I had never seen it, but his voice, when he spoke, was perfectly quiet.

“Thank you, Jim,” he said aloud. “Run below, then, and lay the wine and glasses. We shall want them presently.”

Captain Smollett, on the quarter-deck, had already taken in the doctor’s look and the whiteness of mine. He gave his orders for shortening sail and laying our course to clear the island on the eastward side as coolly as if it had been an ordinary landfall on the coast of England. Then, and not till then, he glanced at me.

“Hawkins,” says he, “bide in the cabin till we come.”

I went down the companion on legs that were still not my own. The cabin was warm and close after the night air, the stern windows open upon the moonlit wake. I set out bottle and glasses with hands that rattled them together, and then I stood in the dimness and listened to the cheer that followed the captain’s address to the men. I could not distinguish the words, but I knew what the cheer must mean—that the land was sighted, that grog was to be served, and that the gentlemen would presently come below to drink the crew’s health, as a blind for what was truly toward. Somewhere above me, I was sure, a pair of dark eyes were searching the deck for a boy who was no longer there.

The gentlemen came at last, with Hunter, Joyce, and Redruth in attendance upon the squire; and the moment the door was shut, Dr. Livesey took me by both shoulders and looked me in the face.

“Now, Jim,” says he. “From the beginning.”

I began where I ought not—with the end. “Silver knows I heard him,” I said. “Dick found me when he went for the apple. Hands would have killed me on the spot, but Silver held him off. Then he made me promise to say nothing till he gave me leave, with Hands’s knife at my back.”

The squire started up, red in the face. “Made you promise, the villain—”

“Sit down, sir, if you please,” said the captain, “and let the boy get it out.”

So I told the whole of it, as short as I could, from Flint and his old crew to the vote of death when the treasure should be aboard, and the special fate Silver had kept for Mr. Trelawney with his own hands. Nobody interrupted me. The squire’s colour went and came; the doctor sat with his chin upon his fist; and Captain Smollett, very upright by the table, never took his eyes from my face.

When I had done, there was a silence, and then the captain asked, “And this promise? What kept you from us when you got to the doctor?”

I hung my head. “I was afraid of what Silver said—that they would rise at once and murder you all in the dark. And—and he had just saved my life from Hands.”

“A promise dragged out of a boy at the point of a knife,” said the doctor, “is a promise to no man, Jim. Put that out of your head.”

“Amen to that,” says the captain, “but it has cost us the one thing we most needed, and that is time. Silver knows the boy has heard him, and by now, unless I’m much mistaken, Silver knows the boy has come aft. We cannot sit here and pretend ignorance with a man of his cut.”

“Then let us go up and seize him!” cried the squire.

“With what, sir?” returned the captain. “You, I, the doctor, your three servants, and this boy—seven in all, as I make it—and Silver’s party in possession of the forecastle. No, sir. We will not go up to be butchered on the companion steps like sheep. Hunter, Joyce, Redruth—are you Mr. Trelawney’s men in this, or are you not?”

“We are, sir,” said Hunter at once, “to the last.”

The others said the same, and Redruth, who was the oldest of the three, quietly moved to stand by the door.

“Then we make the stern of the ship our fort,” said the captain, “and we take it now, before they choose the moment for us.”

He unlocked the arms-chest as he spoke. At that instant the cheerful noise upon deck, which had gone on through all our talk, died away into an unnatural quiet. There came a soft pad of bare feet overhead, the faint clink of iron against a belaying pin, and then, unmistakably, the slow thump of a crutch upon the planks above the companion.

Captain Smollett crossed the cabin in two strides and slid the bolt home. At the table Squire Trelawney was already ramming down a charge with a hand that shook more from rage than fear, and Dr. Livesey, cool as if he were loading for a morning’s shooting at home, had a musket across his knee and the powder-horn between his teeth. I stood between them with a brace of pistols in my belt that felt as heavy as anchors, and my apple, still unbitten, rolling forgotten under the table.

A knock came upon the door—not loud, but firm.

“Cap’n Smollett,” says Silver’s voice, civil as ever, “there’s been some foolishness of a lad’s dreaming, sir, and I’m come aft to set it right. Let me in, and we’ll talk it over like seamen.”

“You may talk from where you are, Silver,” says the captain.

A pause. “You’ve heard a hard story of old John,” says he, and I could almost see the smile. “Boys in barrels hears what pleases their fears, sir. Give me the lad, and nobody need be the worse.”

“You will not have the lad,” said the captain. “And you will take your men forward off the quarter-deck.”

The smile went out of the voice. “Then it’s open between us, is it, sir?”

“It is what you have made it,” says the captain.

We heard the crutch retreat, step by deliberate step, up the companion. Captain Smollett drew back the bolt again.

“They expect us to sit below and be smoked out like wasps,” he said. “We go up now, gentlemen, while they draw off, and we hold the quarter-deck. Quarter-deck commands the waist. Keep together, and no man fires till I give the word.”

We went up in a body, the captain first with a pistol in either hand, the doctor and squire behind him with their muskets, and the three servants closing the rear. I kept where the doctor had put me, close against his left side, for my pistols were more burden than use in hands that would not stop trembling.

The moon was now high and the island lay before us in a glory of silver and shadow—two low hills close together, and behind them a third, greater cone with the mist still smoking about its peak. The *Hispaniola*, with her helm lashed and her topsails drawing faintly in the night wind, crept on through shining water toward it. And across the waist, drawn back in a black, silent body by the mainmast, stood the mutineers with cutlasses in their hands. Silver was in front of them upon his crutch, one great fist resting on a cutlass hilt; Hands snarled at his right shoulder, and behind them both I saw the terrified white face of Dick, dragged thus far by the company he had chosen.

Captain Smollett raised his musket, and the doctor and squire levelled theirs beside him. Not a word was spoken from either side of the ship. There we stood, gentlemen and mutineers, with the breadth of the moonlit waist between us, and waited for the first man to lift a hand.
